140 m (150 yd) (TriCa) |

| References | [\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-OFTTR-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) |

The **Trichy assault rifle** (TAR), sometimes known as the **Tiruchi assault rifle**,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) is an [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")\-made [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") chambered for the [7.62×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739mm "7.62×39mm") round. The TAR is based on the [AR-M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1 "AR-M1"), produced by [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") manufacturer [Arsenal AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_AD "Arsenal AD"). Developed between 2011 and 2015, [Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli "Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli") (OFT) began manufacturing TARs in 2017.

The TAR was developed to reduce dependence on [imported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Import "Import") AR-M1s under the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") self-reliance policy. The TAR has been adopted by most [Indian law enforcement agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_India "Law enforcement in India").

Prior to the TAR's introduction, India largely used foreign-made [AK-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalashnikov_rifle "Kalashnikov rifle") rifles. Around 500,000 M1s were reportedly imported by India from Bulgaria in 2021 for use by the [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") (CAPF) and [Indian police forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) As of May 2025, India is the [second-largest arms importer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_industry#World's_largest_arms_importers "Arms industry") after [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"), accounting for 8.3% of the arms trade, according to research data from the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-5) To reduce dependence on importing small arms from other countries, part of the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") policy called for self-sufficiency to manufacture firearms in India.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-6)

OFT announced the manufacture of an indigenous AK-based assault rifle in 2011.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) The AR was named Trichy after OFT to recognise the factory's contribution in developing and manufacturing the rifle.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-9) Some TARs were made in 2012 to be tested.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) These early TARs were tested by the [Border Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF), the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Reserve_Police_Force "Central Reserve Police Force") (CRPF), the [Indo-Tibetan Border Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Tibetan_Border_Police "Indo-Tibetan Border Police") and the [Sashastra Seema Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sashastra_Seema_Bal "Sashastra Seema Bal").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

Development started in 2015[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) with a production line established in 2017.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-13) That March, 200 TARs were acquired by the [Chhattisgarh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhattisgarh_Police "Chhattisgarh Police")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyF-14) as part of the 216th Ordnance Factories Day celebration.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15) Concerns were raised at the time, prior to manufacture, that OFT was experiencing manpower decline, leading to a decline of employees at the company.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16) The [All India Defence Employees Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_India_Defence_Employees_Federation "All India Defence Employees Federation"), the [Indian National Defence Workers' Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Defence_Workers%27_Federation "Indian National Defence Workers' Federation"), and the [Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Pratiraksha_Mazdoor_Sangh "Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh") stated their opposition to importing small arms with the unions hoping that more orders for the TAR would be approved, retaining employees at OFT.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg/250px-Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)

A [CISF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") officer practices with the TAR at a shooting range.

In November 2017, the CRPF conducted field tests to determine the suitability of the TAR with 15,000 rounds fired[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) at the [CRPF Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRPF_Academy "CRPF Academy") in Kadarpur, [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana") with no reports of the rifle jamming.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-17) Other tests conducted included the TAR being fired from mud, rain and saltwater and from being dropped to test reliability and accuracy.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) 100 TARs were ordered afterwards.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) In February 2018, further tests were conducted by the CRPF at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar with an order of 6,167 TARs placed afterwards.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) At the time, the CRPF tested the Trichy with the Ghatak, the [Joint Venture Protective Carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Venture_Protective_Carbine "Joint Venture Protective Carbine") and the [INSAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle")1C.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-19) In March 2020, the CRPF acquired the first 500 out of 6,167 TARs sold to them.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11)

In January 2019, the TAR was delivered to the BSF, with its Additional Director General Nasir Kamal receiving the first rifle from the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate_of_Ordnance_/(Coordination_%26_Services/) "Directorate of Ordnance (Coordination & Services)")'s Director General Saurabh Kumar.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) It was reported in the same month that the [Jharkhand Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jharkhand_Police "Jharkhand Police") would acquire TARs for anti-Naxalite operations.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-JPR-20) The TAR was displayed for the first time at the Pragati Maidan in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi") for the 5th International Police Expo and the 4th India Homeland Security Expo.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-21) In February 2020, the TAR was on public display at the Defence Expo at [Lucknow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucknow "Lucknow"), [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) It was reported at the time that the TAR was offered to the [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) OFT reported in March 2021 that around 11,500 TARs were supplied for a total of [Rs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupee_sign "Rupee sign") 1.60 billion during fiscal year 2020–21.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-23)

In January 2021, the TriCa (Trichy Carbine) Carbine was unveiled.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) Tests were conducted where 2,000 rounds were fired with no stoppages.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) That August, OFT announced that the TAR could use the [ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"), which was presented by OFT general manager Sanjay Dwivedi.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-UBGL-24) A TAR variant with a downfolding stock was presented publicly.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25) This variant was sought out by the [Railway Protection Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Protection_Force "Railway Protection Force") aside from the CAPFs.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-26) In December 2021, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") placed an order of 100 TriCa carbines.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NSGTriCa-27) On April 2022, the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") (KP) ordered 92 TriCa carbines.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) According to OFT, the [Greyhounds unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhounds_/(police/) "Greyhounds (police)") ordered 44 TARs.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) In July 2022, the [Government of Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Kerala "Government of Kerala") received a request from KP to procure 250 TARs with side folding stocks;[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-29) they received the TriCa carbines in May 2025.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30) According to the [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India "Advanced Weapons and Equipment India")'s (AWEIL) 2022–2023 Annual Report, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") and the [Andhra Pradesh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andhra_Pradesh_Police "Andhra Pradesh Police") conducted tests on both the TAR and the TriCa carbine.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-31)

In January 2023, the [Central Industrial Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") (CISF) received TARs manufactured from [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-32) That April, Minister of State for Defence and Tourism [Ajay Bhatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajay_Bhatt_/(politician/) "Ajay Bhatt (politician)") visited OFT, where he witnessed the TAR being manufactured in the factory while briefed on OFT's research and development work.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-33) The following January, BSF procured further TARs featuring bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34) The Government of Kerala published an approved plan for the KP to acquire 30 TARs.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-35) In November 2023, the Trichy was on display at the Dasara Exhibition in [Mysore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysore "Mysore"), [Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka "Karnataka") as part of an effort to raise awareness on crime and public safety.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-36) In a July 2024 interview with Rajesh Choudhary, Chairman and Managing Director of AWEIL, he said that the TAR continues to be in demand with CAPFs and reported that an export order was made for the rifle.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEILI-37) In May 2025, it was reported that the Assam Forest Department and the [Central Bureau of Narcotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bureau_of_Narcotics "Central Bureau of Narcotics") made orders for the TriCa carbine.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30)

Initial versions of the TAR were produced by using [FN FAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FN_FAL "FN FAL")\-based receivers and were using 7.62x39 mm magazines.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) In 2012, there were reports that the prototypes jammed during testing due to the rate of fire being 800 rounds per minutes instead of 600 rounds per minute to match with the AK-47.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) It was initially expected that the rate of fire would be at 650 rounds per minute.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

The current version of the TAR is based on the AR-M1[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-38) with a machined receiver instead of stamped sheet to ensure the rifle has high accuracy and reliability.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) The TAR can be outfitted with [picatinny rails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picatinny_rail "Picatinny rail") on the upper handguard to attach scopes if requested.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18)

In July 2021, it was reported that the TARs used by the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") are effective in [Naxalite-Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naxalite%E2%80%93Maoist_insurgency "Naxalite–Maoist insurgency") [counterinsurgency operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterinsurgency "Counterinsurgency").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-39)

On August 2025, a TAR was secured from pro-Maoist communist [Naxalite fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Guerrilla_Army_/(India/) "People's Liberation Guerrilla Army (India)") in Chhattisgarh’s [Narayanpur district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narayanpur_district "Narayanpur district").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-cp-40)

The TAR can fire with single, burst and full automatic mode.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyDemand-41) OFT reported that the TAR can be adopted with single shot mode only for police forces in cities and urban areas.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-OFTTR-1) While it has an effective range of 300 to 350 metres,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEIL2122-42) the range can be up to 500 metres if the rifle is used in full auto.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)

OFT claimed that the TAR is functionally on par with the AK-47.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22)

The TAR can be equipped with several [underbarrel grenade launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenade_launcher "Grenade launcher"), including the [ARDE UBGL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"),[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-43) the [GP-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GP-25 "GP-25"), the GP-30 and the Arsenal M6 UBGL.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) The TAR can use bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34)

[Magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_/(firearms/) "Magazine (firearms)") for the TAR are supplied by Nilkamal Limited.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-44) Magazines made for [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47")\-based assault rifles can also be used.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

[7.62×39 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739_mm "7.62×39 mm") ammunition of all types can be used for the TAR.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

TAR variants. From top to bottom: TAR side folding stock, TAR down folding stock and TriCa carbine.

### Trichy assault rifle

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Trichy assault rifle")\]

Main variant with a fixed stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (side)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (side)")\]

TAR variant with a side folding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (down)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (down)")\]

Unveiled on August 2021, it is a TAR variant with a downfolding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25)

It's sometimes referred to as a variant with an underfolding stock.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)

### Trichy Carbine (TriCa)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Trichy Carbine (TriCa)")\]

Unveiled on January 2021, the TriCa weights 3.17 kg and is marketed as a compact weapon for vehicle crews, paratroopers and special forces units.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) The TriCA's firing range is from 150-175 metres.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) A muzzle device is installed on the barrel to minimize muzzle flash and sound when it's fired.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2)

The TriCa is a clone based on the Arsenal AR-M14SF, but the muzzle device is based on the AKS-74U.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-47)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-MILMAG-46)

It is sometimes known as **Baby TAR** or **TAR-3**.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)

Bulk orders for Indian-made AK-47s have stabilised the Atmanirbhar design plan, helping the Ordnance Factory Board innovate and create a compact version of the assault rifle

'Baby TAR', India’s smallest assault rifle

[![Image 4: Sandeep Unnithan](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/reporter/201901/image005_0-770x433-profile_image_one_to_one_1.jpg?VersionId=.pasKkvdD84ULmLha3vENVAV69BnJMOd&size=50:50)](https://www.indiatoday.in/author/sandeep-unnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")

[Sandeep Unnithan](https://www.indiatoday.in/author/sandeep-unnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")[](https://twitter.com/@SandeepUnnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")

Delhi,UPDATED: Jan 25, 2021 20:23 IST

![Image 5](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/mediamanager/india_today_insight.jpg?IzvocAu7gyMv.UA3nBmTl5xRnm990vx3)It’s laptop-sized, can be carried inside a coat and can spit AK-47 bullets out at the rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. Meet the ‘Baby TAR’, India’s smallest assault rifle. Developed by the Indian Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappali, the weapon is a compact version of the legendary AK-47, which the factory has been mass-producing since 2017. This in-house OFB innovation comes soon after the Indian Army unveiled a 9x19mm carbine developed in-house.

advertisement

The TAR-3, a compact, fully automatic version of the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), recently passed a series of trials at the Ordnance Factory Trichy (OF Trichy). A dozen prototypes have been produced during the lockdown. The weapon is currently undergoing ‘unofficial trials’ with the Indian Army, where three prototypes are believed to have fired over 2,000 rounds each without stoppages.

The ‘Baby TAR’ fires the same 7.62x39 mm cartridge as the AK-47—this ammunition is in widespread production and use, thereby easing logistics. It uses the AK-47’s distinctive 30-round curved box magazine and features a commonality of parts with existing weapons. Its designers chopped down the AK-47’s 16-inch barrel, producing a weapon with an 8.3-inch barrel and an effective range of 150 metres. The TAR-3 is 19.2 inches long with its stock folded, and at 2.7 kg (unloaded), is one kg lighter than the AK-47. It has a monoblock receiver, shockproof polymer lower parts and two Picatinny rails that can mount a variety of sights and scopes.

ALSO READ | [The Indian Army’s ‘General Kalashnikov’ gives it a new 9 mm sub-machine gun](https://www.indiatoday.in/india-today-insight/story/the-indian-army-s-general-kalashnikov-gives-it-a-new-9-mm-sub-machine-gun-1759202-2021-01-14)

Its designers say it is ideal for users like special forces and counter-terrorist operators who want compact, concealable weapons but with the firepower of a full-sized AK-47. The assault rifle is also suitable for aircraft, tank and vehicle crews. Significantly, the weapon was developed as an unsolicited design—without waiting for army General Staff Qualitative Requirements (GSQRs), which usually is the start point for weapon development. To do so, the factory used the experience it gained from mass producing the Trichy Assault Rifle, a wholly indigenous copy of the AK-47.

Designers at OF Trichy appear to have solved a problem that stumped the gun designers of the DRDO’s now-discarded INSAS carbine variant in the 1990s—how to reduce the barrel heating and the excessive sound and flash produced when an assault rifle bullet is fired from a short barrel. The DRDO did it by switching over to a smaller bullet, the 5.56x30 round used in the JVPC carbine. The Baby TAR designers solved the problem by used internal metal reflectors to insulate the foregrip from the barrel and by designing, in-house, a compact flash hider at the barrel muzzle. The gun can presently fire four full magazines—around 120 rounds—without the barrel heating. This development is noteworthy because it means Indian designers now understand the ‘know-why’, rather than just the ‘know-how’ that they would have gained from a licensed production.

advertisement

**Compacting the AK**

The Soviet Union began producing compact, stubbier versions of its AK-74 rifle (an AK-47 evolution firing the 5.45x39 mm cartridge) in the 1970s. Copies of this compact assault rifle have been famously attached to Osama bin Laden, ISIS chief Abu Bakr Al Baghdadi and more recently, Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko. Compact versions of the AK-47 believed to have been produced in the frontier regions of Pakistan, have been recovered by Indian security forces from terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir in recent months.

Trichy is one of two Indian ordnance factories already mass-producing Indian versions of the legendary Kalashnikov (the original weapon was never patented and is freely made by countries across the world). The ‘Ghatak’, a copy made by Rifle Factory Ishapore, did not find as much favour. The full-sized TAR is believed to be a copy of the Bulgarian AR-M1, itself a licensed copy of the Kalashnikov. Over 500,000 Bulgarian weapons have been imported by India’s central, state and paramilitary forces over the past decade—the TAR, which began bulk production in 2017, has also helped reducing imports from that east European country. OF Trichy has developed four variants of the rifle, with fixed, side-folding, under-folding and telescoping butts. Nearly 20,000 weapons have been delivered to the Indian police, paramilitary and central armed police forces. Interestingly, each TAR costs around Rs 55,000—far less than the licensed AK-203 to be produced by Indo-Russian Rifles, which will cost upwards of Rs 75,000. And the compact version could cost less than the full-length TAR.

advertisement

The compact TAR’s arrival has added to growing numbers of indigenously designed small arms. From a virtual drought a few years back, there are now multiple indigenous designs available, chambered for various cartridges. Besides the Army’s 9x19mm carbine, the DRDO has developed a variant firing a 5.56x45 mm cartridge, for a different Army requirement. The JVPC, a DRDO-OFB carbine, passed Army and MHA development trials last year. Bengaluru-based small arms start up SSS Defence has its own designs for weapons, chambered for 5.56x45 and 7.62x39 cartridges, and an upgrade kit for existing AK-47 variants. All these designs, of course, are at the prototype stage and will need to fire several thousand rounds before they are fit for mass-production and induction.

The **IWI Tavor**, previously designated as the Tavor TAR-21 (Tavor Assault Rifle – 21st century),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-4) is an Israeli [bullpup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullpup "Bullpup") [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO"), designed and produced by [Israel Weapon Industries (IWI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Weapon_Industries "Israel Weapon Industries"). It is part of the Tavor family of rifles, which have spawned many derivatives of the original design.

The Tavor TAR-21 can also be mounted with the [M203 grenade launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203_grenade_launcher "M203 grenade launcher"), designated as the GTAR-21. A compact variant with a 380 mm (15 in) barrel is also available, designated as the CTAR-21. A designated marksman rifle variant with a folding under-barrel [bipod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipod "Bipod") and [Trijicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trijicon "Trijicon") [ACOG 4×](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Combat_Optical_Gunsight "Advanced Combat Optical Gunsight") magnification sight was also made but later phased out in favour for the Tavor TAR Flattop.

Built around a long-stroke piston system (as found in the [M1 Garand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1_Garand "M1 Garand") and [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47")), the Tavor is designed to maximise reliability, durability, simplicity of design, and ease of maintenance, particularly under adverse battlefield conditions.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5)

In 2009, the [Tavor X95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavor_X95 "Tavor X95") (also known as the Micro Tavor or MTAR) was selected by the [Israel Defense Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces "Israel Defense Forces") to gradually replace the [M16 assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M16_rifle "M16 rifle") and [M4 carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_carbine "M4 carbine") variants as the standard-issued weapon of the Israeli infantry by the end of 2018. The first X95 bullpup rifles were issued to infantry units in 2013.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-inn.co.il2-6) A report published on the IDF's website revealed the IDF plans to continue acquiring the Micro Tavor and equipping combat units with it.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-isrDef8sep21-7)

History
-------

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_%287%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_%287%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_/(7/).jpg)

Tavor (X95 and CTAR-21 variants) in use with Israel's [Golani Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golani_Brigade "Golani Brigade")

[Israel Military Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Military_Industries "Israel Military Industries") (the small arms branch of IMI was privatized into [Israel Weapon Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Weapon_Industries "Israel Weapon Industries")) initiated the Tavor development team in 1995, under the direction of gun designer Zalmen Shebs.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8)

The objective of the project was to create an assault rifle that was more reliable, durable, and easier to maintain than the [M4A1 carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4A1_Carbine "M4A1 Carbine"), while also being better suited to close-quarters combat and mechanized infantry roles. As a result, they hoped that the weapon would be officially adopted by the Israel Defense Forces.

Due to the military's close-quarters and mechanized infantry requirements, the project team selected a bullpup design that would allow the weapon to be compact while keeping a long barrel able to achieve ballistically favourable high muzzle velocities.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8) A long-stroke piston system, similar to that found in the AK-47 and M1 Garand, was selected to ensure the weapon's reliability under adverse conditions.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1)

### Trials and service

By 1997,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-9) early prototypes were produced,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-10) with the Tavor prevailing over the [M4A1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4A1_Carbine "M4A1 Carbine") in a series of trials conducted during 2001 and 2002 by the Israel Defense Force. Qualities tested included Mean Rounds Between Failures (MRBF), reliability, ergonomics during long marches, and ease-of-maintenance.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5)

As part of initial testing by Israel Defense Forces' infantry units, the TAR-21 was distributed to members of the training company of the Tzabar Battalion from the [Givati Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givati_Brigade "Givati Brigade") who were drafted in August 2001. They received their rifles in November 2001 during basic training. Initial testing results were favourable – the TAR-21 was found to be significantly more accurate and reliable (as well as more comfortable) than the [M4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_carbine "M4 carbine") during extensive field testing.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-11)

Issues with fine sand entering the Tavor TAR's chamber, which were identified over the two years of testing, were rectified by numerous small adjustments. A number of other improvements and changes to the design were also made between 2001 and 2009.

The Tavor CTAR-21 saw combat service in [Operation Cast Lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Cast_Lead "Operation Cast Lead"), used by [Givati Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givati_Brigade "Givati Brigade") and [Golani Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golani_Brigade "Golani Brigade"), and the soldiers reported the Tavor bullpup assault rifles functioned flawlessly.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-12)

In November 2009, the IDF announced that the Tavor X95 would become the standard infantry weapon of the IDF, with the addition of an integrated grenade launcher.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-dover.idf.il2-13) A gradual changeover has begun in 2006 and expected completion among front line troops was to be by the end of 2018.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-sadj2-14)

In December 2012, the IDF announced that they would begin equipping and training their new reserve forces with the Tavor TAR-21.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-15)

The first Tavor X95s were issued to new recruits of a main IDF infantry brigade in 2013, replacing the M16.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-inn.co.il2-6) In 2014 the IDF announced that in the future (from as early as the end of 2014) some infantry units could start to be issued some numbers of an improved X95, which will have a longer 38 cm (15 in) barrel (instead of the original 33 cm barrel) and a lighter trigger pull.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-16)

On 8 September, the _IsraelDefense_ website reported that the IDF plans to continue acquiring the Micro Tavor, quoting from a report posted on the IDF's Hebrew website on 7 September regarding a multi-year plan. The rifle is to be distributed to combat troops of relevant units in upcoming rounds of recruitment. The weapons division of the Ground Forces Command was quoted as saying that it's "very satisfied by its capabilities... the rifle performs very well and has proven itself."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-isrDef8sep21-7)

Design details
--------------

The Tavor is a [bullpup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullpup "Bullpup") [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle"), capable of both [semi-automatic fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_firearm "Semi-automatic firearm") and [fully automatic fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_firearm "Automatic firearm"). Due to its bullpup design the [receiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_/(firearms/) "Receiver (firearms)"), bolt carrier group, and [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_/(firearms/)#Function_and_types "Magazine (firearms)") are placed behind the pistol grip. This shortens the firearm's overall length without sacrificing barrel length. As a result, the Tavor provides [carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbine "Carbine") overall length, yet can achieve [rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle "Rifle") muzzle velocities if equipped with a rifle-length barrel.

### Long-stroke piston system

The Tavor uses a non-lubricated [long-stroke piston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas-operated_reloading#Long-stroke "Gas-operated reloading") system, as found in the [M1 Garand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1_Garand "M1 Garand"), [IMI Galil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Galil "IMI Galil"), and the [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK_47 "AK 47").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1) Like in the AK-47, the long-stroke piston mechanism contributes to the extreme forcefulness of the TAR-21's extraction and chambering.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-sadj2-14) The Tavor's attachment of the piston to a heavy bolt carrier, and the extension of the mainspring into the hollow stem of the bolt carrier, bears a familiar resemblance to the internal mechanism of the AK-47.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1)

### Ambidexterity and modularity

The Tavor has ejection ports on both sides of the rifle so it can easily be reconfigured for right or left-handed shooters. However, this process requires partial disassembly, so it cannot be quickly reconfigured while the rifle is in use.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-youtubevideo2-17) An issue related to this is the original plastic cover on the unused ejection can allow gas to escape during the course of fire. Due to the bullpup design, this vents right under the shooter's face, causing issues such as inhaling ejection gases and the fouling of glasses and face with ejection debris. The issue is exacerbated when the weapon is suppressed. This has been addressed by various non-factory solutions which increase sealing of the unused port.

Its ambidextrous [fire mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_fire "Selective fire") selector above the pistol grip has a [semi-automatic mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_firearm "Semi-automatic firearm") and a [fully automatic mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_firearm "Automatic firearm").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-weapon2-18) The Tavor features a self-contained, drop-in [trigger group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigger_group "Trigger group") so that the trigger group can be changed or replaced without the use of additional tools.

### Chambering, cartridges and ammunition feeding

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_%2811%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_%2811%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_/(11/).jpg)

A [Nahal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahal_Brigade "Nahal Brigade") soldier conducts firing drill with a CTAR-21

The Tavor is primarily chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO") and uses [STANAG magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STANAG_magazine "STANAG magazine"), conversion kits for [9×19mm Parabellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9%C3%9719mm_Parabellum "9×19mm Parabellum") and [5.45×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.45%C3%9739mm "5.45×39mm") calibre are also available.

The IDF uses both 3.6-gram (55 gr) M193 and 4.0-gram (62 gr) M855 5.56×45mm rounds. M193 rounds are used by regular infantrymen for better terminal effects at shorter distances, while the heavier M855 is used by sharpshooters.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-sadj2-14)

### Last round bolt-open catch

The Tavor features a last round bolt catch, whereby the bolt holds open after the last round discharges.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-19) This is a request of modern armies, as it helps to allow soldiers to know when their magazine empties and to reduce reloading times during combat while also not requiring manual action cycling after.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-20)

### Barrel

The Tavor barrels are made from CrMoV steel and cold-hammer-forged (CHF) on the premises of the IWI factory in [Ramat HaSharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramat_HaSharon "Ramat HaSharon"). The TAR-21 barrel is 18 inches (457 mm) in length and is chrome-lined for durability and corrosion resistance. The barrel features six grooves in a one in seven inch (178 mm) twist, or 32 calibres right hand [twist rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifling "Rifling").

The barrel is fitted with a 'birdcage' style [flash suppressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_suppressor "Flash suppressor"), which can be fully disassembled without the need for additional tools.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-sadj2-14)

### Reliability, ease-of-maintenance and waterproofing

The design objectives of the Tavor aimed for reliability and ease-of-maintenance, particularly under adverse or battlefield conditions.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5) According to Russell C. Tilstra, the Tavor is "easily considered more reliable" than the M16 and M4 series rifles.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-21)

The Tavor is designed to be easily field-stripped, without the need for any additional tools.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-22)

It is waterproofed and its internal mechanism is sealed from outside elements, so that it can pass [over-the-beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over-the-beach_capability "Over-the-beach capability") requirements.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-23)

Variants
--------

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg)

[Caracal Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracal_Battalion "Caracal Battalion") IDF combat soldier armed with the GTAR-21 which is equipped with a [M203](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203 "M203") grenade launcher

IWI produces the Tavor TAR-21 in different variations as outlined below.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-weapon2-18)

### TAR-21

The Tavor TAR-21 is the standard variant with a 457 mm (18 in) long barrel.

#### GTAR-21

The GTAR-21 has a notched barrel, to accept an [M203 grenade launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203_grenade_launcher "M203 grenade launcher"), or a licensed variant thereof, chambered in [40x46mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40x46mm "40x46mm").

#### CTAR-21

The CTAR-21 is a compact shorter 380 mm (15 in) barrel variant intended for [commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commandos "Commandos") and [special forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_forces "Special forces"), but has become more favoured than the standard TAR-21 throughout the IDF.

#### STAR-21

The STAR-21 is a [designated marksman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_marksman "Designated marksman") variant with folding under-barrel [bipod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipod "Bipod") and [Trijicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trijicon "Trijicon") [ACOG 4×](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Combat_Optical_Gunsight "Advanced Combat Optical Gunsight") magnification sight

### Tavor X95

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_%287a%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_%287a%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_/(7a/).jpg)

Israeli infantry with the [IWI X95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_X95 "IWI X95") "Micro-Tavor"

The X95 (previously known as the **MTAR-21**) is the variant of the Tavor that was selected as the future standard infantry weapon of the IDF in 2009.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-dover.idf.il2-13) In 2013, the X95 was issued for the first time as the standard infantry weapon to recruits of the Givati Brigade.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-24)

With the use of a conversion kit, the X95 can be converted from a 5.56 mm assault rifle to a 9 mm [submachine gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submachine_gun "Submachine gun"). A [suppressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppressor "Suppressor") can also be added to the weapon, as part of the 9 mm conversion kit. A grenade launcher can also be attached to the X95.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-25)

### Tavor 7

The IWI Tavor 7 is derived from the Tavor TAR. Essentially a [battle rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_rifle "Battle rifle"), chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO. It is fully ambidextrous, features a 432 mm (17 in) barrel with a 730 mm (28.7 in) overall length. and a 508 mm (20 in) barrel with an 806 mm (31.7 in) overall length.

### Ukrainian-licensed Tavors

[Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") purchased a license for Tavors to be manufactured by Ukrainian firearm manufacturer [RPC Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPC_Fort "RPC Fort"). As of March 2021, Fort is no longer marketing them.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-FBU-26)

*   **Fort-221** – Ukrainian locally produced version of the CTAR-21 in 5.45×39 mm.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-FBU-26)
*   **Fort-222** – Ukrainian locally produced version of the STAR-21 in 5.45×39 mm.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-27)

### TC-21

The semi-automatic Tavor Carbine (TC-21) was first made available for civilian customers to purchase in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Canada "Wikipedia:Canada") from 2008.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-28) The Canadian civilian version initially shipped with the Mepro reflex sight and a slightly longer barrel to meet the Canadian requirement for non-restricted semi-automatic centrefire rifles to have a barrel length of at least 470 mm. Current versions are shipped with a full-length Picatinny rail, without optics. In Europe, the Czech company Zeleny Sport recently (December 2015) imported Israeli-made TC-21s, equipped with Mepro M5 or M21 reflex sight, which are now available for both civilian and law enforcement customers.

In 2013, IWI started a US subsidiary, IWI US, which is manufacturing the semi-automatic TC-21 as the Tavor SAR for U.S. sales.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-29) The weapon is manufactured with a combination of Israeli and US parts. IWI US had shipped 50,000 Tavor SARs to US civilian customers by early 2016.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-30)

IWI US sells the Tavor SAR in variety of variants:[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-31)

*   **TSB16**: Semi-automatic version of the CTAR-21, with a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB16L**: A TSB16 with left-handed controls pre-installed.
*   **TSB16-BLK**: A TSB16 chambered in [.300 AAC Blackout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.300_AAC_Blackout ".300 AAC Blackout").
*   **TSB17-9**: 9×19 mm submachine gun with a 17 in (432 mm) barrel and a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB18**: 5.56×45 mm rifle with an 18 in (457 mm) barrel and a 27+5⁄8 in (702 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB18RS**: 5.56×45 mm rifle with an 18 in (457 mm) barrel and a 30 in (762 mm) overall length; integrated permanent 2+3⁄8 in muzzle brake and a 10-round magazine to be compliant with laws of certain states. ("RS" stands for Restricted State.)
*   **TSIDF16**: Semi-automatic version of the CTAR-21 without a full-length rail, an integrated MEPRO 21 sight, and a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length; meant to be a semi-automatic replica of the CTAR-21 issued to the IDF.

Note: IWI US sells their Tavor SARs in a variety of colours, including Black (B), Flat Dark Earth (FD), and OD Green (G); the letter "B" subsequent to "TS" in the rifles' designations can be switched with any of the colours' respective letters.

#### Aftermarket parts

A significant aftermarket of spare and replacement parts has developed around the Tavor rifle family, including the development of [match grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match_grade "Match grade") [accurizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accurizing "Accurizing") triggers for the bullpup rifle that are produced by manufacturers such as Geissele Automatics and double stage trigger pack TAV-D from Shooting Sight.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-israeldefense.com-32)

Shlomi Sabag, Deputy CEO of IWI, says that one of the indicators of the success of the rifle in the shooting sports or civilian market is the fact that "an aftermarket of products associated with the Tavor bullpup rifle, like triggers, has evolved very quickly".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-israeldefense.com-32)

Sights
------

The **ITL MARS** (multi-purpose aiming reflex sight) is a gun [sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sight_/(device/) "Sight (device)") that combines two sighting devices, a [reflex sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex_sight "Reflex sight") and a [laser sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_applications#Laser_sight "Laser applications"), as well as a backup [iron sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_sights "Iron sights"). It is designed and produced by [ITL Optronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ITL_Optronics&action=edit&redlink=1 "ITL Optronics (page does not exist)") company, based in [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"). The laser may be either visible or [infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") and can be activated as needed via a pressure switch. It has been purchased by a number of forces including the U.S. military for its [M16 series weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M16_rifle "M16 rifle"), Israel for its [IMI Tavor TAR-21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21 "IMI Tavor TAR-21") rifle, and India (locally manufactured under license as raptor sight) for its [INSAS rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle"), as well as other commercial customers.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-33)

_[American Rifleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rifleman "American Rifleman")_ magazine awarded the Tavor SAR the 2014 Golden Bullseye Award as its Rifle of the Year.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-35)

_[Shooting Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shooting_Illustrated&action=edit&redlink=1 "Shooting Illustrated (page does not exist)")_ magazine named the Tavor X95 as its 2017 Rifle of the Year.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21#cite_note-36)

The Tavor family of assault rifles has seen, perhaps the most widespread use among the various Special Forces and paramilitary units of India, compared to any other foreign rifle in recent times (save for the ubiquitous and never-dying Kalashnikov)…making it just a few steps short of gaining SLR-like status and renown among armed units in India (those steps I’ve explained in the last part of this article).  
![Image 1](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Tavor-1-218x145.jpg)

**First off, a little bit about the rifle itself and it’s Israeli history:**

The Tavor is a bullpup design with a long-stroke piston, with the charging handle on the left side and an ambidextrous design overall (with ejection ports provided on both sides, enabling the conversion of a right-handed operation to a left-handed one on the same rifle with just a partial disassembly of the receiver). All Tavor variants produced so far are chambered for the 5.56x45mm NATO round as standard – although variants that can accept 9x19mm and Russian 5.45x39mm feed also exist, but mainly for the civilian market. The bullpup concept was adopted for it’s ability to provide carbine-esque dimensions of the gun body whilst still being able to attain the higher muzzle velocities, effective range and accuracy afforded by having a longer barrel – with a bullpup, one can have a rifle-length barrel attached to a carbine-length gun body.

The first successful iteration of the family, the TAR-21 (standing for Tavor Assault Rifle – 21st Century), was designed by a (then known as) Israel Military Industries (IMI) team lead by Zalmen Shebs, beginning in 1995 – with the intent of providing a more compact, more reliable and easier-to-maintain replacement for the M4 carbines used as standard-issue by the Israel Defense Forces.

![Image 2](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal_s_Special_Forces_Conduct-218x145.jpg)

Even though the TAR-21 had conducted firing trials as early as 2001-2002, it was only by 2009 that the improved X-95 variant (otherwise known as Micro Tavor or MTAR) was finally accepted by the Older Forum as the future replacement of the M4A1 in Israeli infantry service.

Coming to India – the Tavor & it’s variants have seen ample use. From the snowy Himalayas to the hot deserts of Thar and the tropical forests of the Red Corridor, this Israeli rifle has proven itself as a favorite. What follows is an account of the varied Tavor variants and their varied users in India – and where the Tavor has potential to serve next.  
![Image 3](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/1512579302739-150x150.png)  
_Para commandos with the TAR-21. Pic credit: Shatrujeet009_

TAR-21

The first & most basic iteration of the family, also the most widely used in India. The biggest user of this variant, and one that gave the Tavor the opportunity to grow roots in India, is undoubtedly the Para Special Forces (Para-SF) of the Army. The first deal for Tavors was signed in 2002 – reportedly for over 3,000 rifles. This variant with the standard 18″ (457mm) barrel, overall length of 28.3″ and an empty weight of 3.27kg is also the base variant used by SOFs under the other two services, namely the Garuds and MARCOS. The Para-SF TAR-21s are mostly seen with the MARS reflex sight from ITL Optronics of Israel – which combines a laser pointer into the same mount as the sight – saving space for other attachments (especially on early-model TAR-21s which do not have extensive Picatinny rails). Whereas the Garud & MARCOS TAR-21 variants are equipped with the Mepro MOR system (which combines three elements – a reflex sight, a visible laser and an IR laser, in the same module) from Meprolight, another Israeli optronics manufacturer.

_![Image 4](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Para-_SF_TAR-21_1-356x200.png)_

_Para-SF operator with TAR-21 & MARS reflex sight, Pic credit: Discovery Channel_

The Special Frontier Force (SFF) is also known to use a limited quantity of TAR-21s. The Sagar Prahari Bal (SPB) is another user. The National Security Guard (NSG) is also known to maintain a number of Tavors for training and weapon-familiarization purposes, although these have never been seen.

The use of TAR-21 among the Para-SF, Garuds & MARCOS continues to grow: making it the go-to rifle of Indian Special Forces units.

_![Image 5](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/MARCOS_Wular_Lake_Jammu_Kashmir_Tavor_TAR-21_Mepro_MOR_sight-337x220.jpg)_

_MARCOS with the TAR-21 (and Mepro MOR) operating near the Wular Lake in Kashmir_

CTAR-21

This is a ‘Carbine’ variant of the basic TAR-21, the difference being in the shorter 15″ (380mm) barrel and the resulting drop in weight to 3.18kg and overall length to 25.2 inches. This iteration makes the CTAR more suited for Close Quarters Combat applications (or operation from within vehicles) than the full-length TAR-21. The only service that routinely makes use of this variant in India are the Garud commandos of the IAF.

_![Image 6](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/photo-1-220x220.jpg)_

_Garud CTAR-21, with Mepro MOR_

The utility of the CTAR today has been more or less nullified with the advent of the improved X-95 variants. So the only ones that want shorter barrels are those who wish to convert their existing TAR-21s into a CQC-oriented role, without having to buy a whole new system (like X95).

**GTAR-21**

The Grenade-launcher variant. Comes with a notched barrel designed to accept attachment of the US M203 40mm grenade launcher (which, like for M4, requires removal of the lower handguard in order to seat). Also comes with a leaflet sight for the launcher, mounted on top of the barrel or on top of the handguard. But the GTARs in India, seen in use by Paras, Garuds, MARCOS as well as the SPB, instead use the Turkish MKEK T-40 launcher.

![Image 7](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/C2_Mf_C-_YWEAAln_Y0-313x220.jpg)

_Para-SF GTAR-21 (foreground). Note the barrel shroud with holes._

The Paras continue to use the barrel shroud that comes with the T-40 (but has no utility on the Tavor as the attachment of the launcher, unlike as on the M16, does not require the complete removal of the standard handguard –upper and lower–, therefore on the Tavor, the shroud does not actually cover the barrel). But the Garuds, MARCOS and SPB have understandably discarded the shroud.

![Image 8](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/6os_Sg-331x220.jpg)

_SPB personnel with GTAR-21, without the shroud_

**STAR-21**

The Marksman variant. The only user of this type in India, as far as this writer knows, are the Garuds. The STAR is basically the same as the TAR, except that the folding bipod is provided as standard equipment which ups the weight to 3.67kg (not that the bipod can’t be used on the TAR, as the Paras amply demonstrate it can), and was intended to make use of the Trijicon ACOG (4x) or a similar magnifier. But the STAR-21s in Indian service have been seen with scopes of higher power – namely the Nimrod 6×40 from IWI, otherwise seen only on the Galatz DMR (the Galil sniper variant). This entails an increase in weight as well.

_![Image 9](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/garuds_2_1.jpg)_

_Garud operator with STAR-21, and the Nimrod 6×40 scope_

**X-95: The Next Generation Tavor**

The X95 (previously known as the Micro Tavor or MTAR, and sometimes incorrectly referred to as the MTAR-21) is an improved Tavor – it is smaller, lighter and infinitely more adaptable. Offered in barrel lengths of 13″, 15″ as well as 16.5″ (not counting the 11″ 9mm SMG variant), the X95 is available in overall lengths ranging from 22.8″ to 26.4″. Originally, it was developed as an even more compact variant of the CTAR-21, but at least as far as the Older Forum is concerned, it was far more successful than any other Tavor variant – the X95 is now the standard-issue assault rifle of the Israeli military.

![Image 10](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/israel-356x212.jpg)

Design changes include modifications to the stock, the trigger guard, the receiver, and the handguard – making it more or less a complete overhaul of the TAR-21 design. Although the biggest operational difference is likely to be the location of the charging handle – which is now right above the trigger group, as opposed to the TAR-21’s handle which was closer to the muzzle. Multiple P-rails were now standard fit – with the top cut into two sections, a medium-length rail over the trigger group and a pair of short ones over and under the handguard.

_![Image 11](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/idf_weapon_style_12_by_guy191184-d5kivu1-295x220.jpg)_

_Tavor X-95 and an M4 CQB variant in use by IDF_

In this initial variant, the X95 entered service with various Paramilitary & Police Special Units of India under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). Among CAPFs, both the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), especially it’s CoBRA units geared for jungle warfare, as well as the Border Security Force (BSF) have adopted the X-95. Other units such as the Chattisgarh Police’s Special Task Force (STF), the Punjab Police’s Special Weapons And Tactics (SWAT) division and Uttarakhand Police commandos are also known to operate the X95, no doubt drawing from the experience of operating and training with CoBRA/other CAPF units under the MHA umbrella. All X-95s used in India are only ever seen with the Mepro MOR sight.

_![Image 12](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/CRPF_COBRA_Tavor_X95.jpg)_

_CRPF_ CoBRA _operator with the Tavor X-95_

Previously, India’s state-run Ordnance Factories Board (OFB) had entered into an agreement with Israel for the local production of the Tavor X95 under the name “Zittara”. While some prototypes and limited production models exist, this program never actually took off and essentially nothing came of it – prompting IWI to seek a private-sector partner for manufacturing their weapon systems in India: Punj Llyod (detailed in a further section).

The recent-most production variant of the Tavor is the latest iteration of the X-95 (which so far has not been bought by anyone in India). What’s new in this update is that the split-section P-rails are gone, and in came a single full-length 12’O clock rail, and short rails at the other three crucial spots around the handguard as well: the 3’O clock, 6’O clock and 9’O clock positions.

_![Image 13](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/IWI_Tavor_X95_136-356x178.jpg)_

_Latest X-95 variant. Note the P-rail system_

**Tavor 7 AR**

The latest Tavor version on the market – not yet in full scale production, but has sure managed to grab eyeballs the world over. Biggest difference being that this is the first Tavor chambered for the large(r) 7.62x51mm NATO round. The development of the 7AR was aimed both at the US civilian market, and military requirements that call for heavier calibers than the usual 5.56 Nato. The 7AR is the biggest & heaviest Tavor variant so far, with several design changes over the TAR-21 family, mainly the relocation of the charging handle (thanks to experience gained in X95 development). The 7AR weighs some 4.1kg without the magazine, comes with a 4-point variable gas regulator and two barrel lengths – a 17″ (432mm) and a 20″ (508mm). The rifle comes with an overall length of 28.4″.

_![Image 14](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/1509382325_IWI_TAVOR_7_AR_6-330x220.jpg)_

_TAVOR 7 – IWI_

**PUNJ LLYOD RAKSHA SYSTEMS (PLRS) Pvt. Ltd.**

PLR(S) was established in early 2016 as a 51:49 Joint Venture between India’s Punj Llyod Industries Ltd. (PLIL) and Israel Weapon Industries (IWI), with the intent of manufacturing the many IWI weapon systems, components & accessories meant to be used by both Indian and non-Indian customers. The product portfolio here includes the Tavor TAR-21, X-95, Galil Sniper and the Negev LMG – as well as over a dozen different types of weapon accessories. As of mid-2017, PLRS has begun manufacturing of certain components at their Gwalior factory, aimed for integration with weapon systems produced by IWI elsewhere.

_![Image 15](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/IWI_Punj_Llyod.jpg)_

_PLRS Product Portfolio, Pics credit: INDRA Network_

Judging by both the advertised capabilities of the weapon and it’s widespread service in Indian conditions (and favored by Special Forces operators), the following are this writer’s pointers to where the Tavor has more potential, and what, in the writer’s opinion, needs to be done to improve their working in our military/CAPFs service.

The Army’s requirement for 250,000 rifles of 7.62x51mm caliber represents a unique opportunity for IWI to find a large order from a tried-and-tested customer for its new Tavor 7 AR rifle. If the Indian Amy does indeed select the 7 AR as the future standard-issue rifle for frontline Indian infantry, this production order will cement the future of the PLRS Joint Venture and provide a much-needed breather for Punj Llyod. Sans any large orders, this JV is likely to meet the same fate as the OFB’s Zittara venture – and once again, the less-than-satisfactory performance of OFB is all that the Indian military will have on table when it comes to buying Made in India firearms. However, PLRS has made a smart decision in deciding to not wait for Indian orders before starting component production – so even if they do not get large scale orders from within India, PLRS has potential to be global chain supplier for IWI for their products sold all over the world

If Army adopts 7AR as standard-issue (which would automatically entail local manufacturing as production of 7.62 Tavor by PLRS has been okayed), that will massively increase the weapon’s popularity and availability (making it the modern-day SLR analogue as far as Indian Army is concerned, from the current Special Forces-exclusive weapon that it is today). If this does happen, it will speak volumes about Bullpup designs in general: with the world’s two largest Land Armies using Bullpups as standard-issue (PLA uses the QBZ-95).

The latest iteration of the Tavor X-95 can be an ideal replacement for the 9x19mm Heckler & Koch MP-5s used by the CRPF’s Quick-Reaction Teams (QRT) that operate in the state of Jammu & Kashmir.

![Image 16](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/CRPF_QRT_UCP_ACU_MP-5_A2.jpg)  
Special Forces operators can be encouraged to increase the utility & adaptability of their existing TAR-21 variants with the adoption of the Flattop P-rail attachment, which provides a single full-length 12’O clock rail for TAR-21s which otherwise don’t have the long rails.  
![Image 17](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/wm_8222485-356x188.jpg)

![Image 18](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/wgc_ufc_tar21_flattoprail_02-356x200.jpg)  
Only two of India’s five CAPFs (Central Armed Police Forces) are currently known to operate the Tavor/X-95, namely the CRPF and the BSF. The other three, especially the ITBP, can also be viable customers for the X-95 and/or the Tavor 7 AR, as a replacement for their old INSAS and 1A SLR rifles. The CISF’s possibility of engaging in firefights in urban locations might make them a customer for the compact X-95 as well, as a replacement for their AKMs and INSAS.

Ending this article/opinion piece with this beautiful image of the X-95 from the Canada-based Caliber Magazine…

![Image 19](https://www.strategicfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/DSC_0083_2.jpg)

Written by @[Gessler](https://www.strategicfront.org/forums/members/parthu.29/)
