The **IWI Tavor**, previously designated as the Tavor TAR-21 (Tavor Assault Rifle – 21st century),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-4) is an Israeli [bullpup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullpup "Bullpup") [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO"), designed and produced by [Israel Weapon Industries (IWI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Weapon_Industries "Israel Weapon Industries"). It is part of the Tavor family of rifles, which have spawned many derivatives of the original design.

The Tavor TAR-21 can also be mounted with the [M203 grenade launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203_grenade_launcher "M203 grenade launcher"), designated as the GTAR-21. A compact variant with a 380 mm (15 in) barrel is also available, designated as the CTAR-21. A designated marksman rifle variant with a folding under-barrel [bipod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipod "Bipod") and [Trijicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trijicon "Trijicon") [ACOG 4×](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Combat_Optical_Gunsight "Advanced Combat Optical Gunsight") magnification sight was also made but later phased out in favour for the Tavor TAR Flattop.

Built around a long-stroke piston system (as found in the [M1 Garand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1_Garand "M1 Garand") and [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47")), the Tavor is designed to maximise reliability, durability, simplicity of design, and ease of maintenance, particularly under adverse battlefield conditions.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5)

In 2009, the [Tavor X95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavor_X95 "Tavor X95") (also known as the Micro Tavor or MTAR) was selected by the [Israel Defense Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces "Israel Defense Forces") to gradually replace the [M16 assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M16_rifle "M16 rifle") and [M4 carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_carbine "M4 carbine") variants as the standard-issued weapon of the Israeli infantry by the end of 2018. The first X95 bullpup rifles were issued to infantry units in 2013.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-inn.co.il2-6) A report published on the IDF's website revealed the IDF plans to continue acquiring the Micro Tavor and equipping combat units with it.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-isrDef8sep21-7)

History
-------

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_%287%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_%287%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_The_Strongest_Trees_in_the_Golan_Heights_/(7/).jpg)

Tavor (X95 and CTAR-21 variants) in use with Israel's [Golani Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golani_Brigade "Golani Brigade")

[Israel Military Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Military_Industries "Israel Military Industries") (the small arms branch of IMI was privatized into [Israel Weapon Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Weapon_Industries "Israel Weapon Industries")) initiated the Tavor development team in 1995, under the direction of gun designer Zalmen Shebs.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8)

The objective of the project was to create an assault rifle that was more reliable, durable, and easier to maintain than the [M4A1 carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4A1_Carbine "M4A1 Carbine"), while also being better suited to close-quarters combat and mechanized infantry roles. As a result, they hoped that the weapon would be officially adopted by the Israel Defense Forces.

Due to the military's close-quarters and mechanized infantry requirements, the project team selected a bullpup design that would allow the weapon to be compact while keeping a long barrel able to achieve ballistically favourable high muzzle velocities.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8) A long-stroke piston system, similar to that found in the AK-47 and M1 Garand, was selected to ensure the weapon's reliability under adverse conditions.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1)

### Trials and service

By 1997,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-9) early prototypes were produced,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-10) with the Tavor prevailing over the [M4A1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4A1_Carbine "M4A1 Carbine") in a series of trials conducted during 2001 and 2002 by the Israel Defense Force. Qualities tested included Mean Rounds Between Failures (MRBF), reliability, ergonomics during long marches, and ease-of-maintenance.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5)

As part of initial testing by Israel Defense Forces' infantry units, the TAR-21 was distributed to members of the training company of the Tzabar Battalion from the [Givati Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givati_Brigade "Givati Brigade") who were drafted in August 2001. They received their rifles in November 2001 during basic training. Initial testing results were favourable – the TAR-21 was found to be significantly more accurate and reliable (as well as more comfortable) than the [M4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_carbine "M4 carbine") during extensive field testing.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-11)

Issues with fine sand entering the Tavor TAR's chamber, which were identified over the two years of testing, were rectified by numerous small adjustments. A number of other improvements and changes to the design were also made between 2001 and 2009.

The Tavor CTAR-21 saw combat service in [Operation Cast Lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Cast_Lead "Operation Cast Lead"), used by [Givati Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givati_Brigade "Givati Brigade") and [Golani Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golani_Brigade "Golani Brigade"), and the soldiers reported the Tavor bullpup assault rifles functioned flawlessly.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-12)

In November 2009, the IDF announced that the Tavor X95 would become the standard infantry weapon of the IDF, with the addition of an integrated grenade launcher.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-dover.idf.il2-13) A gradual changeover has begun in 2006 and expected completion among front line troops was to be by the end of 2018.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-TAVOR_History-8)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-sadj2-14)

In December 2012, the IDF announced that they would begin equipping and training their new reserve forces with the Tavor TAR-21.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-15)

The first Tavor X95s were issued to new recruits of a main IDF infantry brigade in 2013, replacing the M16.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-inn.co.il2-6) In 2014 the IDF announced that in the future (from as early as the end of 2014) some infantry units could start to be issued some numbers of an improved X95, which will have a longer 38 cm (15 in) barrel (instead of the original 33 cm barrel) and a lighter trigger pull.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-16)

On 8 September, the _IsraelDefense_ website reported that the IDF plans to continue acquiring the Micro Tavor, quoting from a report posted on the IDF's Hebrew website on 7 September regarding a multi-year plan. The rifle is to be distributed to combat troops of relevant units in upcoming rounds of recruitment. The weapons division of the Ground Forces Command was quoted as saying that it's "very satisfied by its capabilities... the rifle performs very well and has proven itself."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-isrDef8sep21-7)

Design details
--------------

The Tavor is a [bullpup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullpup "Bullpup") [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle"), capable of both [semi-automatic fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_firearm "Semi-automatic firearm") and [fully automatic fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_firearm "Automatic firearm"). Due to its bullpup design the [receiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_/(firearms/) "Receiver (firearms)"), bolt carrier group, and [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_/(firearms/)#Function_and_types "Magazine (firearms)") are placed behind the pistol grip. This shortens the firearm's overall length without sacrificing barrel length. As a result, the Tavor provides [carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbine "Carbine") overall length, yet can achieve [rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle "Rifle") muzzle velocities if equipped with a rifle-length barrel.

### Long-stroke piston system

The Tavor uses a non-lubricated [long-stroke piston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas-operated_reloading#Long-stroke "Gas-operated reloading") system, as found in the [M1 Garand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1_Garand "M1 Garand"), [IMI Galil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Galil "IMI Galil"), and the [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK_47 "AK 47").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1) Like in the AK-47, the long-stroke piston mechanism contributes to the extreme forcefulness of the TAR-21's extraction and chambering.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-sadj2-14) The Tavor's attachment of the piston to a heavy bolt carrier, and the extension of the mainspring into the hollow stem of the bolt carrier, bears a familiar resemblance to the internal mechanism of the AK-47.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Future_Weapons_2007-1)

### Ambidexterity and modularity

The Tavor has ejection ports on both sides of the rifle so it can easily be reconfigured for right or left-handed shooters. However, this process requires partial disassembly, so it cannot be quickly reconfigured while the rifle is in use.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-youtubevideo2-17) An issue related to this is the original plastic cover on the unused ejection can allow gas to escape during the course of fire. Due to the bullpup design, this vents right under the shooter's face, causing issues such as inhaling ejection gases and the fouling of glasses and face with ejection debris. The issue is exacerbated when the weapon is suppressed. This has been addressed by various non-factory solutions which increase sealing of the unused port.

Its ambidextrous [fire mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_fire "Selective fire") selector above the pistol grip has a [semi-automatic mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_firearm "Semi-automatic firearm") and a [fully automatic mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_firearm "Automatic firearm").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-weapon2-18) The Tavor features a self-contained, drop-in [trigger group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigger_group "Trigger group") so that the trigger group can be changed or replaced without the use of additional tools.

### Chambering, cartridges and ammunition feeding

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_%2811%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_%2811%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Nahal%27s_Special_Forces_Conduct_Firing_Drill_/(11/).jpg)

A [Nahal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahal_Brigade "Nahal Brigade") soldier conducts firing drill with a CTAR-21

The Tavor is primarily chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO") and uses [STANAG magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STANAG_magazine "STANAG magazine"), conversion kits for [9×19mm Parabellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9%C3%9719mm_Parabellum "9×19mm Parabellum") and [5.45×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.45%C3%9739mm "5.45×39mm") calibre are also available.

The IDF uses both 3.6-gram (55 gr) M193 and 4.0-gram (62 gr) M855 5.56×45mm rounds. M193 rounds are used by regular infantrymen for better terminal effects at shorter distances, while the heavier M855 is used by sharpshooters.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-sadj2-14)

### Last round bolt-open catch

The Tavor features a last round bolt catch, whereby the bolt holds open after the last round discharges.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-19) This is a request of modern armies, as it helps to allow soldiers to know when their magazine empties and to reduce reloading times during combat while also not requiring manual action cycling after.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-20)

### Barrel

The Tavor barrels are made from CrMoV steel and cold-hammer-forged (CHF) on the premises of the IWI factory in [Ramat HaSharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramat_HaSharon "Ramat HaSharon"). The TAR-21 barrel is 18 inches (457 mm) in length and is chrome-lined for durability and corrosion resistance. The barrel features six grooves in a one in seven inch (178 mm) twist, or 32 calibres right hand [twist rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifling "Rifling").

The barrel is fitted with a 'birdcage' style [flash suppressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_suppressor "Flash suppressor"), which can be fully disassembled without the need for additional tools.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-sadj2-14)

### Reliability, ease-of-maintenance and waterproofing

The design objectives of the Tavor aimed for reliability and ease-of-maintenance, particularly under adverse or battlefield conditions.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-Decidedly_Different:_The_IWI_Tavor-5) According to Russell C. Tilstra, the Tavor is "easily considered more reliable" than the M16 and M4 series rifles.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-21)

The Tavor is designed to be easily field-stripped, without the need for any additional tools.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-22)

It is waterproofed and its internal mechanism is sealed from outside elements, so that it can pass [over-the-beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over-the-beach_capability "Over-the-beach capability") requirements.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-23)

Variants
--------

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Pose_for_the_Camera.jpg)

[Caracal Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracal_Battalion "Caracal Battalion") IDF combat soldier armed with the GTAR-21 which is equipped with a [M203](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203 "M203") grenade launcher

IWI produces the Tavor TAR-21 in different variations as outlined below.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-weapon2-18)

### TAR-21

The Tavor TAR-21 is the standard variant with a 457 mm (18 in) long barrel.

#### GTAR-21

The GTAR-21 has a notched barrel, to accept an [M203 grenade launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M203_grenade_launcher "M203 grenade launcher"), or a licensed variant thereof, chambered in [40x46mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40x46mm "40x46mm").

#### CTAR-21

The CTAR-21 is a compact shorter 380 mm (15 in) barrel variant intended for [commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commandos "Commandos") and [special forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_forces "Special forces"), but has become more favoured than the standard TAR-21 throughout the IDF.

#### STAR-21

The STAR-21 is a [designated marksman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_marksman "Designated marksman") variant with folding under-barrel [bipod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipod "Bipod") and [Trijicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trijicon "Trijicon") [ACOG 4×](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Combat_Optical_Gunsight "Advanced Combat Optical Gunsight") magnification sight

### Tavor X95

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_%287a%29.jpg/250px-Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_%287a%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flickr_-_Israel_Defense_Forces_-_Golani_Brigade_Conducts_Exercise_in_Mount_Hermon_Snow_/(7a/).jpg)

Israeli infantry with the [IWI X95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_X95 "IWI X95") "Micro-Tavor"

The X95 (previously known as the **MTAR-21**) is the variant of the Tavor that was selected as the future standard infantry weapon of the IDF in 2009.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-dover.idf.il2-13) In 2013, the X95 was issued for the first time as the standard infantry weapon to recruits of the Givati Brigade.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-24)

With the use of a conversion kit, the X95 can be converted from a 5.56 mm assault rifle to a 9 mm [submachine gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submachine_gun "Submachine gun"). A [suppressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppressor "Suppressor") can also be added to the weapon, as part of the 9 mm conversion kit. A grenade launcher can also be attached to the X95.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-25)

### Tavor 7

The IWI Tavor 7 is derived from the Tavor TAR. Essentially a [battle rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_rifle "Battle rifle"), chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO. It is fully ambidextrous, features a 432 mm (17 in) barrel with a 730 mm (28.7 in) overall length. and a 508 mm (20 in) barrel with an 806 mm (31.7 in) overall length.

### Ukrainian-licensed Tavors

[Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") purchased a license for Tavors to be manufactured by Ukrainian firearm manufacturer [RPC Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPC_Fort "RPC Fort"). As of March 2021, Fort is no longer marketing them.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-FBU-26)

*   **Fort-221** – Ukrainian locally produced version of the CTAR-21 in 5.45×39 mm.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-FBU-26)
*   **Fort-222** – Ukrainian locally produced version of the STAR-21 in 5.45×39 mm.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-27)

### TC-21

The semi-automatic Tavor Carbine (TC-21) was first made available for civilian customers to purchase in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Canada "Wikipedia:Canada") from 2008.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-28) The Canadian civilian version initially shipped with the Mepro reflex sight and a slightly longer barrel to meet the Canadian requirement for non-restricted semi-automatic centrefire rifles to have a barrel length of at least 470 mm. Current versions are shipped with a full-length Picatinny rail, without optics. In Europe, the Czech company Zeleny Sport recently (December 2015) imported Israeli-made TC-21s, equipped with Mepro M5 or M21 reflex sight, which are now available for both civilian and law enforcement customers.

In 2013, IWI started a US subsidiary, IWI US, which is manufacturing the semi-automatic TC-21 as the Tavor SAR for U.S. sales.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-29) The weapon is manufactured with a combination of Israeli and US parts. IWI US had shipped 50,000 Tavor SARs to US civilian customers by early 2016.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-30)

IWI US sells the Tavor SAR in variety of variants:[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-31)

*   **TSB16**: Semi-automatic version of the CTAR-21, with a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB16L**: A TSB16 with left-handed controls pre-installed.
*   **TSB16-BLK**: A TSB16 chambered in [.300 AAC Blackout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.300_AAC_Blackout ".300 AAC Blackout").
*   **TSB17-9**: 9×19 mm submachine gun with a 17 in (432 mm) barrel and a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB18**: 5.56×45 mm rifle with an 18 in (457 mm) barrel and a 27+5⁄8 in (702 mm) overall length.
*   **TSB18RS**: 5.56×45 mm rifle with an 18 in (457 mm) barrel and a 30 in (762 mm) overall length; integrated permanent 2+3⁄8 in muzzle brake and a 10-round magazine to be compliant with laws of certain states. ("RS" stands for Restricted State.)
*   **TSIDF16**: Semi-automatic version of the CTAR-21 without a full-length rail, an integrated MEPRO 21 sight, and a 26+1⁄8 in (664 mm) overall length; meant to be a semi-automatic replica of the CTAR-21 issued to the IDF.

Note: IWI US sells their Tavor SARs in a variety of colours, including Black (B), Flat Dark Earth (FD), and OD Green (G); the letter "B" subsequent to "TS" in the rifles' designations can be switched with any of the colours' respective letters.

#### Aftermarket parts

A significant aftermarket of spare and replacement parts has developed around the Tavor rifle family, including the development of [match grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match_grade "Match grade") [accurizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accurizing "Accurizing") triggers for the bullpup rifle that are produced by manufacturers such as Geissele Automatics and double stage trigger pack TAV-D from Shooting Sight.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-israeldefense.com-32)

Shlomi Sabag, Deputy CEO of IWI, says that one of the indicators of the success of the rifle in the shooting sports or civilian market is the fact that "an aftermarket of products associated with the Tavor bullpup rifle, like triggers, has evolved very quickly".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-israeldefense.com-32)

Sights
------

The **ITL MARS** (multi-purpose aiming reflex sight) is a gun [sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sight_/(device/) "Sight (device)") that combines two sighting devices, a [reflex sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex_sight "Reflex sight") and a [laser sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_applications#Laser_sight "Laser applications"), as well as a backup [iron sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_sights "Iron sights"). It is designed and produced by [ITL Optronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ITL_Optronics&action=edit&redlink=1 "ITL Optronics (page does not exist)") company, based in [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"). The laser may be either visible or [infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") and can be activated as needed via a pressure switch. It has been purchased by a number of forces including the U.S. military for its [M16 series weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M16_rifle "M16 rifle"), Israel for its [IMI Tavor TAR-21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Tavor_TAR-21 "IMI Tavor TAR-21") rifle, and India (locally manufactured under license as raptor sight) for its [INSAS rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle"), as well as other commercial customers.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-33)

*    ![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Flag_of_Honduras_%282022%E2%80%93present%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Honduras_%282022%E2%80%93present%29.svg.png)[Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"): The [Honduran Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduran_Army "Honduran Army") operates the Tavor X95.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-50)
*    ![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/41/Flag_of_India.svg/40px-Flag_of_India.svg.png)[India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"): In late 2002, India signed an ₹880 million (equivalent to ₹3.4 billion or US$40 million in 2023) deal with [Israel Military Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Military_Industries "Israel Military Industries") for 3,070 manufactured TAR-21s to be issued to India's special forces personnel,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-51) where its ergonomics, reliability in heat and sand might give them an edge at close quarters and deployment from inside vehicles. By 2005, IMI had supplied 350–400 TAR-21s to India's northern [Special Frontier Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Frontier_Force "Special Frontier Force") (SFF). These were subsequently declared to be "operationally unsatisfactory". The required changes were made and tests in Israel during 2006 went well, clearing the contracted consignment for delivery.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-DefenseDaily2-52) The new GTAR-21s came with a modified single-piece stock, new sights and Turkish-made [MKEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MKEK "MKEK") [T-40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MKEK_T-40 "MKEK T-40") under-barrel grenade launchers chambered in [40x46mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40x46mm "40x46mm").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-DefenseDaily2-52) In 2011 the rifles were handed over to [Para SF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Para_SF "Para SF") divisions.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-53) A consignment of over 500 Tavor TAR-21s and another 30 [Galil sniper rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMI_Galil#Galil_Sniper "IMI Galil") worth over ₹150 million (US$1.8 million) and ₹20 million (US$240,000) respectively was delivered to the [MARCOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MARCOS "MARCOS") (Marine Commandos) in December 2010.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-54) In 2016, IWI announced that it was establishing a 49:51 joint venture with Punj Lloyd in India, in order to manufacture rifle components in India.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-55)

*    ![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Flag_of_Morocco.svg/40px-Flag_of_Morocco.svg.png)[Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco"): [General Directorate for National Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%BBret%C3%A9_Nationale_/(Morocco/) "Sûreté Nationale (Morocco)") equipped with the Tavor X95. *    ![Image 27](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Flag_of_Nigeria.svg/40px-Flag_of_Nigeria.svg.png)[Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"): The [State Security Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Security_Service_/(Nigeria/) "State Security Service (Nigeria)") employ it as the primary assault rifle[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-59) for their close protection and tactical units replacing the [Uzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzi "Uzi").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-60)
*    ![Image 28](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Flag_of_North_Macedonia.svg/40px-Flag_of_North_Macedonia.svg.png)[North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia"): Used by Rapid Deployment Unit (Tar-21) and Special Anti-terrorist Unit – Tiger (Tavor x95) .[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-61)

*    ![Image 30](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Flag_of_the_Philippines.svg/40px-Flag_of_the_Philippines.svg.png)[Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"): Small quantities in use by special units of the [Philippine Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Marines "Philippine Marines")[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-62) and [Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Drug_Enforcement_Agency "Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency")[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-63) and one PNP SWAT team in Pasig.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-64)
*    ![Image 31](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Flag_of_Portugal_%28official%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Portugal_%28official%29.svg.png)[Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"): Small quantities of the TAR-21 are in use by field and intervention units of the _[Polícia Judiciária](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol%C3%ADcia_Judici%C3%A1ria "Polícia Judiciária")_, like hostage negotiation teams and investigators who usually work alongside other dedicated law enforcement intervention units—the [Special Operations Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grupo_de_Opera%C3%A7%C3%B5es_Especiais_/(Portugal/) "Grupo de Operações Especiais (Portugal)") (GOE) and the [National Republican Guard's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Republican_Guard_/(Portugal/) "National Republican Guard (Portugal)") Special Operations Company (COE); these weapons were initially intended to equip a new unit under the command of the _Polícia Judiciária_ resembling the GOE. The TAR-21 also participated in the competition for the new [service rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_rifle "Service rifle") for the three branches of the [Portuguese Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Armed_Forces "Portuguese Armed Forces") and the Police Special Operations Group (GOE)—a bid that also included the local production of the TAR-21 in Portugal. However, the TAR-21 was excluded from the shortlist. The competition has meanwhile been annulled, after the other contenders and both political and defence critics accused the competition of favouring the [Heckler & Koch G36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heckler_%26_Koch_G36 "Heckler & Koch G36").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-65)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-66)

*    ![Image 37](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Ukraine.svg/40px-Flag_of_Ukraine.svg.png)[Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"): [Yuriy Lutsenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuriy_Lutsenko "Yuriy Lutsenko"), then head of [Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Internal_Affairs_of_Ukraine "Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine"), announced on October 1, 2008, that IWI and Ukrainian state-owned company [RPC Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPC_Fort "RPC Fort") would jointly manufacture Tavor TAR to enter service with special Ukrainian military and police units.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-73)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-74) RPC Fort had displayed working samples of Tavor TARs chambered in [5.45×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.45%C3%9739mm "5.45×39mm") cartridge with [Milkor 40mm UBGL grenade launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkor_40mm_UBGL_grenade_launcher "Milkor 40mm UBGL grenade launcher") to showcase to Ukrainian security forces officers as a means of convincing them to buy Ukrainian-made Tavor TARs for special forces units.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-75) In December 2009, a resolution was adopted to purchase the Fort 221 chambered in 5.45x39 for Ukrainian intelligence/border guard agencies, purchased in small numbers.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-ASF-76) It was subsequently adopted in 2014 for Ukrainian military and police forces.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-ASF-76) Known users include Ukrainian Spetsnaz forces and the Scorpion unit.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-77)
*    ![Image 38](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a4/Flag_of_the_United_States.svg/40px-Flag_of_the_United_States.svg.png)[United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"): In August 2013, IWI US announced that the [Pennsylvania Capitol Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Capitol_Police "Pennsylvania Capitol Police") had adopted the Tavor SAR, a variant specifically designed for the U.S. market.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-78) In July 2014, it was announced that the [Lakewood, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakewood_Township,_New_Jersey "Lakewood Township, New Jersey") Police Department would begin to adopt the Tavor SAR, after the weapon "met the demands and requirements of the Lakewood PD for reliability, ease-of-maintenance, durability and accuracy".[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-79) The [Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo_County_Sheriff%27s_Office_/(Texas/) "Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office (Texas)") in Texas, operate Tavor SAR.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-80)
*    ![Image 39](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Flag_of_Uruguay.svg/40px-Flag_of_Uruguay.svg.png)[Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay "Uruguay"): On 13 October 2021, it was reported that the [Uruguayan Ministry of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Interior_/(Uruguay/) "Ministry of the Interior (Uruguay)") acquired some 200 Tavor X-95s, manufactured by IWI, for the [Uruguayan National Republican Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Uruguayan_National_Republican_Guard&action=edit&redlink=1 "Uruguayan National Republican Guard (page does not exist)") Directorate. Training was carried out by an instructor from IWI, brought especially to Uruguay for that purpose. The [Uruguayan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Police_of_Uruguay "National Police of Uruguay") also purchased thousands of Tavor rifles from IWI.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWI_Tavor#cite_note-isrDefUruguay-81)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli
Company typeGovernment Organisation
IndustryDefence
FoundedTiruchirappalli, India (1966)

Key people

Shirish Khare, IOFS
(General Manager)
ProductsSmall arms

Number of employees

~1500
ParentAdvanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (current)
Ordnance Factory Board (former)
**Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT)**, also called **Ordnance Factory Trichy**, is a small arms factory operated by [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India_Limited "Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited") based in [Tiruchirappalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiruchirappalli "Tiruchirappalli"), [Tamil Nadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_Nadu "Tamil Nadu"), which was previously part of [Ordnance Factory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Board "Ordnance Factory Board") of the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_/(India/) "Ministry of Defence (India)"), [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-1) The company is headed only by an [IOFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOFS "IOFS") officer called General Manager (ex officio [Additional Secretary to Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additional_Secretary_to_Government_of_India "Additional Secretary to Government of India")) who is the chief executive officer, responsible for the overall management of the company.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-2) OFT is the largest [small arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_arms "Small arms") manufacturing company of India and has the most varied range.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-3) Ordnance Factory Tiruchirapalli was in need after the [Indo-Pakistani War of 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1965 "Indo-Pakistani War of 1965"). It was inaugurated on 3 July 1966 by the then Prime Minister of India, [Indira Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi "Indira Gandhi"), [\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-4), and production began in 1967. It was established to increase the small arms production in the country, assisting [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore") and Small Arms Factory, Kanpur. OFT started its production with 9 mm carbines and now manufactures arms ranging from 5.56 mm rifles to rocket launchers, shell launchers, [grenade launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenade_launchers "Grenade launchers"), aviation armament, [naval armament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_armament "Naval armament"), tank armament, anti-aircraft guns, autocannons, automatic rifles, and sniper rifles.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-5) * [IOF .315 sporting rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOF_.315_sporting_rifle "IOF .315 sporting rifle") - A civilian version of the British [Lee–Enfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Enfield "Lee–Enfield") rifle, chambered in the [8×50mmR Mannlicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8%C3%9750mmR_Mannlicher "8×50mmR Mannlicher") cartridge, rather than the [.303 British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.303_British ".303 British") cartridge.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-6) * [INSAS rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle") - The INSAS (Indian Small Arms System) 5.56 mm assault rifle is the standard-issue rifle of the Indian Army. At least 300,000 of these weapons have been sold to the Indian Army.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-7) * [7.62 mm 1A1 rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L1A1_SLR "L1A1 SLR") - Licence produced variant of the British [L1A1 self-loading rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L1A1_SLR "L1A1 SLR"). It was the standard-issue rifle of the Indian Army and has been replaced by the INSAS.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-9) * [7.62 mm PKT gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PK_machine_gun#PKT "PK machine gun") - Indian license produced variant of [PKT machine gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PK_machine_gun#PKT "PK machine gun") mounted on main battle tanks such as [Arjun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_/(tank/) "Arjun (tank)"), [Ajeya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-72 "T-72"), [Bhishma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-90 "T-90") of the Indian Army.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-10) * [7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle "Trichy assault rifle") - A 7.62 mm calibre assault rifle developed by Ordnance Factory Trichy. In use by paramilitary forces such as CRPF, CISF, BSF, etc.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-auto-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-18) Also in use with the State Police Forces of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Kerala, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, among others.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-auto-12)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-19) * [12.7 mm NSV Heavy Machine Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSV_machine_gun "NSV machine gun") - A heavy machine gun, manufactured by OFT, which can be mounted on helicopters, besides land and sea applications.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-hindu-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-21) * [14.5 mm sub caliber device](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=14.5_mm_sub_caliber_device&action=edit&redlink=1 "14.5 mm sub caliber device (page does not exist)") - A training weapon for the crew of T-72 tank for 125 mm gun, in range practice against standard targets, using 14.5 mm armour piercing incendiary tracer bullet with steel case.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-23) * [14.5 mm KPV Heavy Machine Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPV_heavy_machine_gun "KPV heavy machine gun")[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-24) * [Vidhwansak anti-materiel rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vidhwansak "Vidhwansak") - An anti-materiel sniper rifle developed by OFT. In use with the [Border Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force"). The Vidhwansak can be easily changed between three calibers (12.7 mm, 14.5 mm and 20 mm) by replacing the barrel, bolt, magazine and scope without any specialized tools.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-30) * [GSh-23 aircraft cannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gryazev-Shipunov_GSh-23 "Gryazev-Shipunov GSh-23") - An autocannon, for use onboard aircraft. The Ghasha is the gun used on aircraft like the [Tejas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL_Tejas "HAL Tejas"), [MiG-21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiG-21 "MiG-21"), [MiG-27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiG-27 "MiG-27") and [Mi-24 helicopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mil_Mi-24 "Mil Mi-24"),.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-31) * [30 mm automatic cannon 2A42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30_mm_automatic_cannon_2A42 "30 mm automatic cannon 2A42") - Installed in a two-person turret on the [Sarath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMP-2 "BMP-2") mechanised infantry combat vehicle (ICV) and ships.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli#cite_note-hindu-20) * [30 mm auto grenade launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGS-30 "AGS-30") - provides better mobility, longer range, increased rate of fire, and better accuracy during firing. Significantly lighter than its previous version but far more advanced and powerful, it can engage targets at over 2000m. The **AR-M1** is a [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") assault rifle designed primarily for export. It is a modernized derivative of the [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") (specifically the Type 3 variant).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4)

There are two versions of the AR-M1. One chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO"), and the other in the Soviet [7.62×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739mm "7.62×39mm") cartridge.

During the late 1950s, the [Bulgarian People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_People%27s_Army "Bulgarian People's Army") was equipped with [AK-47s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") imported from the Soviet Union. However, by the early 1960s, the Bulgarian government became interested in producing the AK assault rifle domestically.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) Assembly of AKs, initially from imported Soviet parts, began at the [Arsenal AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_AD "Arsenal AD") state arsenal in [Kazanlak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazanlak "Kazanlak").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) By the mid 1960s, the Kazanlak facility was equipped to begin licensed production of the weapon type and its associated parts. Kalashnikov rifles assembled and later manufactured in Kazanlak received the designation _AKK_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) A derivative with a folding stock was also produced under license as the _AKKS_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4)

After the dissolution of the [People's Republic of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria") in the early 1990s, the Kazanlak factory became a [joint-stock company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") known as [Arsenal AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_AD "Arsenal AD").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) Arsenal offered several modernized variants of the AKK for export, which were rebranded as the _AR_ series.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) The _AR_ pattern rifles are AKKs with different furniture and a few unique features, such as polymer stocks and handguards, as well as several external parts copied directly from the [AK-74](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-74 "AK-74") including new flash hiders, sights, gas blocks, bayonet mountings and bayonets.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4) AR-M1 receivers are milled, rather than stamped (unlike the [AKM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKM "AKM")), and are virtually indistinguishable from those of the early pattern Soviet AKs.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4)

A derivative of the AKKS is also offered for export as the _ARF_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Brayley-4)

The following are/were manufacted by Arsenal AD.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-5)

*   AR-M1 / AR-M1F[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-6) - improved AKK copy with a [flash suppressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_suppressor "Flash suppressor"), black polymer stock set, luminous spots on the [iron sights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_sight "Iron sight") and a rail for mounting [optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telescopic_sight "Telescopic sight"). Chambered in [5.56×45mm NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.56%C3%9745mm_NATO "5.56×45mm NATO") and [7.62×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739mm "7.62×39mm").
*   AR-M2 / AR-M2F - improved AK-74 copy like the AR-M1/AR-M1F, but with a shortened barrel, [AKS-74U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-74#AKS-74U "AK-74") front sight base and [muzzle booster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzzle_booster "Muzzle booster")/flash suppressor hybrid.
*   AR-M4SF - extremely short development of the AR-M1 with [red dot sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_dot_sight "Red dot sight"), provision to mount a [night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_vision "Night vision") [vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night-vision_device "Night-vision device") or [laser sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_sight "Laser sight"). Chambered in 5.56×45mm NATO[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-Honduras-7) and 7.62×39mm.
*   AR-M7F - like the AR-M1, but with an [AK-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-101 "AK-101")\-style folding stock.
*   AR-M9 / AR-M9F - improved AK-74 copy like the AR-M1/AR-M1F, features a thumb-operable [fire selector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_fire "Selective fire") and a different style polymer stock set.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-SAS_26-8)
*   AR / AR-F - improved [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") copies with black polymer lining and optional luminous sights.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-10)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-11)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-12)
*   [Trichy assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle "Trichy assault rifle") - Indian clone of the AR-M1 series.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1#cite_note-14)

**Demand of TAR among Central Reserved Forces**

TAR or Trichy Assault Rifle is a product from erstwhile Ordinance Factory Trichy and now part of AWEIL. The development of the assault rifle was started in 2015 and a production line was established in 2017. The first batch of 200 TARs were delivered to Chandigarh police in March 2017. In November 2017, the CRPF tested the rifle’s functionality and its reliability. Over 15,000 rounds were fired to test the TAR’s life cycle and over 2,400 rounds to test its reliability. In February 2018, the TAR underwent field trial at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar. After regressive trials, the CRPF had placed an order for 6167 rifles TAR.

In January 2024, it was reported that BSF is acquiring 125 TAR rifles along with bayonets and other accessories. BSF has experience with operating TAR and has inducted the assault rifle into service earlier. Other Central Armed Police Forces which include SSB, ITBP & CISF has also procured TAR in some significant numbers. Police forces in several states have also inducted TAR under their modernisation scheme.

**TAR : Specifications**

The Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) is a 7.62X39mm powerful automatic weapon designed to destroy the enemy by fire in single and burst firing mode.  It has an effective range of 350m. Its light weight and modular design make it suitable for the counter-insurgency and counter-terror operations. It comes with foldable and fixed butt type, depending upon the requirement. The foldable butt version is helpful in quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty. The overall length of TAR-Down folding butt is 900mm in butt open condition and 650mm in butt folding condition. The rifle weighs 3.4kg and features a curved magazine with 30 rounds.

The rifle has mono-block receiver body & fibre reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts. It also has a customised version with single round firing mode for police forces. It also features Tritium filled Sources for night firing and picatinny rail for mounting optical sights. It can also be fitted with Under barrel grenade launcher.

TAR very closely resembles Bulgarian Arsenal AR-M1F41. There is minor difference in the gas block & cleaning rod of the assault rifles. There is also some noticeable difference in the pistol grip. TAR is being supplied to paramilitary forces to reduce imports from Bulgaria. The unique feature of TAR is that it provides 12 O’clock rails on upper handguard which is not available in any other AKM copy. TAR is 7.62x39mm assault rifle, similar in calibre to AK-203. In fact TAR is almost equivalent to AK-103 and very close to AK-203 in terms of performance.

In boost to Atmanirbhar Bharat, security forces to get India-made Israeli assault rifles
========================================================================================

 

Special forces and others using these assault rifles used to import them from the Israel Weapons Industry, a former Israeli government firm that was privatised in 2005.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 

[Snehesh Alex Philip](https://theprint.in/author/snehesh-alex-philip/)

 

15 February, 2021 09:07 am IST

Text Size: A- A+

 

**New Delhi:** In a boost to the ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ initiative, India-made Israeli Tavor X 95 rifles are now being supplied to central forces and various state police teams, ThePrint has learnt.

Until now, special forces and others using these assault rifles used to import them from the Israel Weapons Industry (IWI), a former Israeli government firm that was privatised in 2005.

The Indian Army has also issued a fresh Request for Information (RFI) to fast-track procurement (FTP) of 93,895 carbines, after the last process, under which UAE firm Caracal was shortlisted, was [scrapped](https://theprint.in/defence/govt-plans-to-scrap-2-defence-deals-under-foreign-procurement-could-go-atma-nirbhar-way/503522/).

Show Full Article

The Army has issued RFI to all major foreign small arms manufacturers, including Caracal, Colt, SiG Sauer, Beretta and Kalashnikov. But the significant change in FTP this time is that the RFI has also been sent to multiple Indian firms like the Ordinance Factory Board, Reliance Defence, SSS Defence, Bharat Forge of the Kalyani Group and the Adani-PLR Systems, besides others.

“Under the FTP process, it is usually ‘Buy Global’ category, as the forces buy a global product off the shelf which is then supplied to, in a specific short period. But this time, Indian firms will be participating in the FTP process for carbines,” said a source in the defence and security establishment.

The front runner is likely to be the Adani-PLR Systems, which is fielding the Israeli Galil Ace 21 carbine that is now manufactured in India.

The Ace 21 was chosen by the Army in an earlier attempt (2013-14) to buy carbines, but the deal could not go through because of single vendor situation, a development which is not allowed under the Indian defence procurement rules.

The IWI, however, did not take part in the FTP (2017) because it was eyeing a deal for assault rifles (won by an American firm) and the Light Machine Guns (LMGs) — that it had won and is in the process of delivering to the Army.

Sources said that a large tender for over 3 lakh carbines is also in the process and could be issued later this year. This would be a ‘Make in India’ initiative.

ThePrint, in September last year, had reported that the Caracal deal was being scrapped. By December, it was [reported](https://theprint.in/defence/uae-firm-caracal-to-bring-small-arms-portfolio-under-make-in-india-looks-to-salvage-army-deal/555134/) that the UAE firm had offered to manufacture them in India.

### **Made in Indian Tavors**

The Adani-PLR Systems also manufactures the 56×45 mm chambered Tavor X 95 which are used by the special forces and others. These rifles come with ‘Made in India’ markings and were showcased during the recently-held Aero India 2021.

Sources said that the CISF has procured these ‘Made in India’ rifles, along with other state police forces. They also said that Adani-PLR Systems is in the process of setting up India’s first private barrel manufacturing plant in Gwalior. With this, the indigenous manufacture of rifles will go up to about 75 per cent.

The Gwalior facility would be functional by the end of this year and it is expected that other Indian private small arms players will be using it, rather than importing barrels from outside the country.

*   Copied
    

TIRUCHY: Ordnance Factory Tiruchy (OFT) on Thursday handed over the first consignment of 500 assault rifles to CRPF. Trichy Assault Rifles or TAR, as these are called, are the indigenous version of AK-47 rifle. Shirish Khare, GM, OFT  handed over the rifles to DS Rawat, DIG, CRPF. OFT started development of the rifle in 2015, and established a production line in 2017. The first batch of 200 TARs was delivered to Chandigarh police in March 2017. In November 2017, the CRPF tested the rifle for functionality and reliability. It was subjected to a life cycle test by firing 15,000 rounds in one go.

In February 2018, the TAR was deployed for field trial at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar. Following this, order for 6167 rifles were placed.OFT would supply TARs in both fixed and foldable butt models, sources said adding that the latter was in the development stage. The TAR is compatible with GP-25, 30 and UBGL M-6 grenade launchers.

OFT has so far supplied more than 10,000 rifles to Central Armed Police Forces including the BSF, SSB, ITBP & CISF. Police force in several States have also inducted TAR under their modernisation scheme.   
OFT has also taken up research and development projects such as the trial of 7.62X39mm TAR Carbine(long barrel firearm) and 40X46mm UBGL (Underbarrel Grenade Launcher) for TAR/AK 47, which after induction would serve as an import substitute.

Special Service and Features
Launch of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) Down Folding Butt Version
प्रविष्टि तिथि: 26 AUG 2021 12:51PM by PIB Chennai

In commemoration of 75 years of independence, Ordnance Factory, Tiruchirappalli launched Down folding butt version of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle on 25th August 2021.  At present, Ordnance Factory, Tiruchirappali, is manufacturing TAR Rifles in two variants i.e. Fixed butt and side folding butt versions.

    The 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) is a powerful individual automatic weapon designed to destroy the enemy by fire in single and burst firing mode.  It is a single shot Rifle in normal mode and it can be used in burst mode also.  By firing in burst mode in short series, group or single targets at a range up to 500m can be destroyed.  However, the destructive effect of the TAR is up to a range of 1350m.

          Ordnance Factory, Trichirappallin developed and manufactured TAR  Down folding butt version to meet the customer requirement as some of the CAPF units, State Police and RPF required the Down folding butt version for quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty.

  The overall length of TAR-Down folding butt is 900mm in butt open condition and 650mm in butt folding condition.

 The Down folding butt version of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle launched by Shri Sanjay Dwivedi, IOFS, General Manager, Ordnance Factory, Trichirappalli and Shri Rajiv Jain, IOFS, Addl. General Manager, Shri A.K.Singh, IOFS, Addl.General Manager Shri V. Gunasekaran, IOFS, Joint General Manager, Shri S. Krishanaswamy, IOFS, Joint General Manager and other Officers of OFT attended the function.

Atmanirbhar Bharat: indigenous defence manufacturing powers India’s rise as global exporter
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Author:** [DD India](https://ddindia.co.in/author/?author=DD+India "DD India")

![Image 19: Atmanirbhar Bharat: indigenous defence manufacturing powers India’s rise as global exporter](https://ddindia.co.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/ChatGPT-Image-Nov-20-2025-06_14_30-PM.png)

India’s push for self-reliance in defence has entered a new phase, with indigenous manufacturing and exports posting their highest figures so far. Defence production reached ₹1,27,434 crore in 2023-24 — a sharp jump from ₹46,429 crore in 2014-15 — driven by a decade of reforms aimed at reducing import dependence and strengthening local industry. The steady rise in the defence budget, which now stands at ₹6.81 lakh crore for 2025-26 compared to ₹2.53 lakh crore in 2013-14, reflects the government’s long-term strategy of building a technologically advanced and globally competitive military ecosystem.

The formation of seven new defence companies from the erstwhile Ordnance Factories, DRDO’s innovation grants, and the active participation of more than 16,000 MSMEs have further diversified the sector. Now, both public and private sectors are driving year-on-year growth, with the private sector’s production share rising from 21% to 23% in the past year– a clear sign of the blossoming defence ecosystem. Today, at least 65% of defence equipment is manufactured domestically, a striking turnaround from the earlier dominance of imported systems.

**Driving Modernisation and Export Expansion**

This era of accelerated production is paralleled by vibrant export growth. Once confined to a minor role, India’s defence exports have surged, now crossing ₹23,622 crore in FY 2024-25—an impressive 12.04% year-on-year increase and a testament to the sector’s global competitiveness. These exports now reach over 100 nations, ranging from strategic platforms and sub-systems to vital components, with private industry contributing the lion’s share at ₹15,233 crore. The Defence Public Sector Undertakings themselves registered a 42.85% growth in exports, with products like bulletproof jackets, patrol boats, helicopters, radars, and lightweight torpedoes cementing India’s status as a reliable partner in the world’s defence supply chain.

Strategic reforms have been central to this progress. The government’s simplification of licensing, the introduction of an end-to-end digital portal for export authorisations, and the rationalisation of procedures have unlocked new avenues for fast, efficient trade. Through these measures, India’s defence diplomacy has also grown in stature, as exported platforms come paired with training, logistics, and support packages that build trust and foster long-term international partnerships.

**Enabling an Innovative and Integrated Future**

At the heart of these achievements are reforms focused on ease of doing business, research and development, and the encouragement of industry-academia collaboration. Initiatives such as the ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Scheme, the extension of liberalised FDI norms, and support for MSMEs and start-ups are nurturing a fertile environment for technological advances and product innovation. The government’s ambition is clear: to further expand annual defence manufacturing to ₹3 lakh crore and defence exports to ₹50,000 crore by 2029. With new investment opportunities arising from 788 industrial licenses issued to 462 companies, and a record 193 contracts signed in 2024-25, of which 177 went to the domestic industry, the sector’s momentum is unmistakable.

The Standard in Modern Bullpup Service Carbines
-----------------------------------------------

The Tavor X95 is the modern bullpup carbine series from IWI US, chambered in 5.56, .300BLK, and 9mm. Upgrades were implemented from the original TAVOR SAR. These updates include an updated fire control trigger pack with a lighter 5-6 lb. trigger pull, repositioning of the ambidextrous magazine release to an AR-15 familiar location, a forearm/handguard with Picatinny rails at the 3, 6, and 9 o’clock positions under removable rail covers, relocation of the charging handle closer to user for better control, a modular pistol grip design that can be swapped between the cutlass and traditional styles, and a lower profile bolt release button to reduce unintentional bolt closures. Multi-caliber and multi-length, the X95 is a proven multi-national service rifle. **(Note: New production is currently only available in 5.56 NATO)**

## **Atmanirbhar Bharat in Defence: Historical Context and** **Contemporary Implications for India’s Strategic Autonomy**

### Abhimanyu [1] *


**ABSTRACT**

This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the historical aspect and current scenario of
the Indian defence sector. The analysis underscores the potential opportunities that the "Make
in India" initiative presents, including the development of indigenous manufacturing
capabilities, the promotion of public-private partnerships, and the engagement of small and
medium enterprises (SMEs) in defence production. The paper outlines the structure of the
Indian defence industry, which includes Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs),
Ordnance Factories (OFs), and private sector players, alongside academic institutions like
DRDO that contribute to research and development. The paper emphasizes the need for a
strategic vision that prioritizes domestic demand while simultaneously positioning India as a
competitive player in the global defence market. By fostering an environment that encourages
innovation, investment and collaboration the "Make in India" campaign can effectively
transform the Indian defence sector, ultimately contributing to national security and economic
prosperity.


_**Keywords:**_ _Atmanirbhar Bharat, Defence Procurement, Indigenous Manufacturing, Make in_
_India, Self-reliance_


he "Make in India" campaign launched by the Government of India, represents a
transformative initiative aimed at repositioning the country as a global manufacturing
# T hub and a favourable business destination. This ambitious program is particularly

focused on the defence sector, where India currently holds the dubious distinction of being
the world's largest arms importer. The Indian government is determined to establish a robust
and advanced defence industry that not only enhances self-reliance in defence production
but also fosters economic growth and technological innovation. In this modern world of 21st
century, nations provide protection to their people while ensuring their success, strength and
sovereignty and defence establishment is such a segment which ensure this. Along with
providing protection to its citizens, the defence sector also defines the regional and global
sphere of influence of any country. A strong defence shows the domination of the country on
the world stage. If defence sector is solely dependent on imports, no country can dream of
becoming a world leader. Being self-sufficient in defence to be the most important thing for
any country to compete at the international level. Defence establishments of our country is a
major spending sector of Indian economy where total Defence Budget for 2024-25 (Ministry

effective modernization of the armed forces, as suggested by the parliamentary Standing
Committee on Defence (SCOD), which has recommended that the defence budget should be
at least 3% of the GDP. This is the highest spending in comparison to any sector. But as we
have said, self-reliance is very important in defence and India has still not become fully selfreliant in this. As an independent nation, India has also fought wars with Pakistan and
China. In recent times, border skirmishes with India's neighbours are constantly increasing
whether it is the India-China standoff in Aksai Chin or the India-Pakistan standoff in 2019.
Apart from these, the threat of Naxalites, Maoists and many such internal threats is also
increasing. Which showed the importance of a strong defence force to India. This paper aim
to analyse the historical context of India's defence industrial base and its evolution since
independence and explore the potential benefits of public private partnerships in defence
production and technology transfer.

**REVIEW OF LITERATURE**
**Lieutenant General (Dr.) VK Saxena** in his paper **"Atmanirbharta in Defence: How has**
**been the Journey So Far? Where are we Headed"** offers a critical analysis of India's
progress towards self-reliance in the defence sector through initiatives like Make in India
and Atmanirbhar Bharat. It highlights the historical challenges faced in defence
manufacturing and procurement, while emphasizing recent policy frameworks such as the
Defence Production and Export Promotion Policy (DPEPP) 2020 and the Defence
Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020. The document underscores the importance of
indigenization, investment in infrastructure, and fostering innovation to enhance domestic
capabilities. Despite notable advancements, the paper identifies significant gaps between
aspirations and outcomes, calling for sustained efforts in policy implementation and
collaboration between public and private sectors to achieve India's defence manufacturing
goals. Overall, it presents a balanced view of the achievements and challenges in the journey
towards a self-reliant defence ecosystem.

**Iskander Rehman** in his paper **“The Military Dimensions of India’s Rise”** discuss about
the India's military rise which is characterized by significant resource accumulation and
modernization efforts, positioning it as a formidable military power. With a substantial
defence budget that has tripled over the past decade, India boasts a large volunteer force and
is actively enhancing its capabilities across the Army, Navy, and Air Force. However, the
military modernization process is uneven, often driven by prestige rather than strategic
coherence, leading to critical shortfalls in equipment and personnel. The lack of a
comprehensive national strategy and bureaucratic inefficiencies further complicate India's
aspirations to transition from a regional to a global military power. To realize its potential,
India must reform its defence acquisition processes and improve civil-military relations,
ensuring that its military resources are effectively translated into operational capabilities and
strategic outcomes.

**Ajay Singh** in his research paper **"Self-Reliance in Indian Defence"** provides a
comprehensive analysis of India's efforts to achieve self-reliance in its defence sector,
particularly in the context of its historical de-industrialization and the need for a robust
technological base. Singh argues that while India has made strides in developing indigenous
capabilities, significant challenges remain, including bureaucratic inefficiencies and a lack
of innovative activities at the factory level. The paper advocates for restructuring the defence
