Other forces
------------

### Special Frontier Force

The Special Frontier Force (SFF) is India's [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") unit. It was initially conceived in the post [Sino-Indian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_war "Sino-Indian war") period as a guerrilla force composed mainly of [Tibetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_people "Tibetan people") [refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugees "Refugees") whose main goal was to conduct covert operations behind Chinese lines in case of another war between the People's Republic of China and India. Later, its composition and roles were expanded.

Based in [Chakrata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakrata "Chakrata"), [Uttarakhand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttarakhand "Uttarakhand"), SFF is also known as the _Establishment 22_.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-222)[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-223) The force is under the direct supervision of the [Research and Analysis Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_Analysis_Wing "Research and Analysis Wing"), India's external [intelligence agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_agency "Intelligence agency").[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-224)

### Special Protection Group

The Special Protection Group (SPG) was formed in 1988 by an act of the Parliament of India to "provide proximate security to the Prime Minister of India and former Prime Minister of India and members of their immediate families (wife, husband, children and parents)". For former Prime Ministers and their dependents, a regular review is held to decide whether the threat to their life is high enough to warrant SPG protection.

### Railway Protection Force

The Railway Protection Force (RPF) was established under the _Railway Protection Force Act 1957_. The RPF is charged with providing security for Indian Railways.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-225) As of March 2020, it had a sanctioned strength of 74,830 personnel, with 61,869 of them on roll.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-226)[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-227)

### National Disaster Response Force

The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is a specialised force constituted "for the purpose of specialist response to a threatening disaster situation or disaster". It is manned by persons on deputation from the various [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces"). At present it has 12 battalions, located in different parts of India.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-228) The control of NDRF lies with the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), which is headed by the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India").

Special Forces
--------------

The [Special Forces of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Forces_of_India "Special Forces of India") are Indian military units[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-229) with specialised training in the field of special operations such as "[Direct action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action_/(military/) "Direct action (military)"), [Hostage rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostage_rescue "Hostage rescue"), [Counter-terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-terrorism "Counter-terrorism"), [Unconventional warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconventional_warfare "Unconventional warfare"), [Special reconnaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_reconnaissance "Special reconnaissance"), [Foreign Internal Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Internal_Defence "Foreign Internal Defence"), [Personnel recovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personnel_recovery "Personnel recovery"), [Asymmetric warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymmetric_warfare "Asymmetric warfare") and [Counter-proliferation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-proliferation "Counter-proliferation")". The various branches include,

*   **Para (Special Forces)**: Formed in 1966, the [Para (SF)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Para_/(Indian_Special_Forces/) "Para (Indian Special Forces)") are the largest and most important part of the Special Forces of India. They are a part of the highly trained [Parachute Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute_Regiment_/(India/) "Parachute Regiment (India)") of the [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army").[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-230)[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-231)[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-232)[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-Understanding_Special_Forces_by_Colonel_Sharma-233) The main aim of having a Parachute Regiment is for quick deployment of soldiers behind the enemy lines to attack the enemy from behind and destroy their first line of defence. Para (SF) conducts an annual series of joint exercises with [US Army Special Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Special_Forces "United States Army Special Forces") called _Vajra Prahar_.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-234)[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-235)[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-236)
*   **Marine Commandos (MARCOS)**:

[![Image 108](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Operation_Sankalp_Joint_Operation_by_IN_and_IAF_and_rescue_crew_of_MV_Ruen.jpg/250px-Operation_Sankalp_Joint_Operation_by_IN_and_IAF_and_rescue_crew_of_MV_Ruen.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Operation_Sankalp_Joint_Operation_by_IN_and_IAF_and_rescue_crew_of_MV_Ruen.jpg)

Marine Commandos being paradropped, rescuing 17 crew members of tanker MV Ruen from pirates as part of [Operation Sankalp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Sankalp "Operation Sankalp")

[Marine Commandos (MARCOS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MARCOS "MARCOS") is an elite special operations unit of the Indian Navy.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-237) It is specially organised, trained and equipped for the conduct of special operations in a maritime environment. The force has gradually acquired experience and a reputation for professionalism over the two decades it has been in existence. Now it is one of the finest Special Forces units in the world and among the few units qualified to jump in the water with a full combat load. The MARCOS are capable of undertaking operations in all types of terrain, but are specialised in maritime operations in Jammu and Kashmir through the [Jhelum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jhelum "Jhelum") River and [Wular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wular "Wular") Lake.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-238) To strengthen its capabilities to carry out special operations, the navy is planning to procure advanced Integrated Combat System (ICS) for the MARCOS. The Navy wants the ICS for effective command, control and information sharing to maximise capabilities of individuals and groups of the MARCOS while engaging enemies.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-239)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] The individual equipment required by the navy in the ICS includes light weight helmets, head-mounted displays, tactical and soft ballistic vests along with communication equipment. The group-level gear requirements include command and control and surveillance systems along with high speed communication equipment.

*   **Garud Commando Force**: The [Garud Commando Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garud_Commando_Force "Garud Commando Force") is the Special Forces unit of the Indian Air Force. It was formed in September 2004 and has a strength of approximately 2000 personnel.\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] The unit derives its name from [Garuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garuda "Garuda"), a divine bird-like creature of Hindu Mythology. Garud is tasked with the protection of critical Air Force bases and installations; search and rescue during peace and hostilities and disaster relief during calamities.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-PIB_Sep_07-240) Garuds are deployed in the Congo as part of the UN peace keeping operations.

Nuclear weapons
---------------

India has been in possession of [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") since 1974. Its most recent nuclear test took place on 11 May 1998, when [Operation Shakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Shakti "Operation Shakti") (Pokhran-II) was initiated with the detonation of one [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_bomb "Fusion bomb") and three [fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_bomb "Fission bomb") bombs. On 13 May 1998, two additional fission devices were detonated. However, India maintains a "no-first use" and a nuclear deterrence policy against nuclear adversaries. Its nuclear doctrine envisages building a credible minimum deterrent for maintaining a "second strike capability" which would be massive and designed to induce unacceptable damage on the enemy.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-241) India is one of only four nations in the world to possess a [Nuclear triad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_triad "Nuclear triad"). India's nuclear missiles include the [Prithvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prithvi_missile "Prithvi missile"), the [Agni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agni_missile_system "Agni missile system"), the [Shaurya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaurya_missile "Shaurya missile"), the [Sagarika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagarika_/(missile/) "Sagarika (missile)"), the Dhanush, and others. India conducted its first test with the [Agni-V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agni-V "Agni-V") in April 2012 and a second test in September 2013. With its 7,000 kilometres (4,300 mi) range, it can carry a nuclear warhead to the east to include all of China, and to the west deep into Europe.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-242) Agni-VI, with a perceived range of 10,000–12,000 kilometres (6,200–7,500 mi) is also under development with features like [multiple independently targetable re-entry warheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_independently_targetable_reentry_vehicle "Multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle") (MIRVs).[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-243)[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-244)

India also had bomber aircraft such as the [Tupolev Tu-142](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupolev_Tu-142 "Tupolev Tu-142") and well as fighter jets like the [Dassault Rafale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Rafale "Dassault Rafale"), [Sukhoi Su-30MKI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-30MKI "Sukhoi Su-30MKI"), the [Dassault Mirage 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_2000 "Dassault Mirage 2000"), the [MiG-29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiG-29 "MiG-29") and the [HAL Tejas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL_Tejas "HAL Tejas") capable of being armed with nuclear tipped bombs and missiles.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-245) Since India does not have a nuclear first use policy against an adversary, it becomes important to protect from a first strike. This protection is being developed in the form of the two layered [Anti-ballistic missile defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ballistic_Missile_Defence_Programme "Indian Ballistic Missile Defence Programme") system.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\][\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-246)

India's [Strategic Nuclear Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Nuclear_Command "Strategic Nuclear Command") controls its land-based nuclear warheads, while the navy controls the ship and submarine based missiles and the air force the air-based warheads. India's nuclear warheads are deployed in five areas:

1.  Ship based mobile, like the [Dhanush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhanush_/(missile/) "Dhanush (missile)"). (operational)
2.  Land-based mobile, like the [Agni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agni_missile_system "Agni missile system"). (operational)
3.  Fixed underground silos (operational)
4.  Submarine based, like the [Sagarika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagarika_/(missile/) "Sagarika (missile)"). (operational)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-India_triad-22)
5.  Air-based warheads of the Indian Air Forces' [strategic bomber force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction#Nuclear-capable_aircraft "India and weapons of mass destruction") like the [Dassault Mirage 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_2000 "Dassault Mirage 2000") and the [Jaguar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEPECAT_Jaguar "SEPECAT Jaguar") (operational)

### India's nuclear doctrine

India has a declared nuclear [no-first-use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_first_use "No first use") policy and is in the process of developing a nuclear doctrine based on "credible [minimum deterrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_deterrence "Minimum deterrence")". In August 1999, the Indian government released a draft of the doctrine[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-NFU-261) which asserts that nuclear weapons are solely for deterrence and that India will pursue a policy of "retaliation only". The document also maintains that India "will not be the first to initiate a nuclear first strike, but will respond with punitive retaliation should deterrence fail".[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-NFU-261)

The fourth [National Security Advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Advisor_/(India/) "National Security Advisor (India)") of India [Shivshankar Menon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shivshankar_Menon "Shivshankar Menon") signalled a significant shift from "[no first use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_first_use "No first use")" to "no first use against non-nuclear weapon states" in a speech on the occasion of the Golden Jubilee celebrations of the [National Defence College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defence_College,_India "National Defence College, India") in New Delhi on 21 October 2010, a doctrine Menon said reflected India's "strategic culture, with its emphasis on minimal deterrence".[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-262) However, whether the policy shift actually took place or not is unclear.[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-263) Some argued that this was not a substantive change but "an innocent typographical or lexical error in the text of the speech".[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-264) India's current PM Modi has, in the run up to the recent general elections, reiterated commitment to no first use policy.[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-265) In April 2013 [Shyam Saran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shyam_Saran "Shyam Saran"), convener of the [National Security Advisory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Advisory_Board "National Security Advisory Board"), affirmed that regardless of the size of a nuclear "attack against India," be it a miniaturised version or a "big" missile, India will "retaliate massively to inflict unacceptable damage".[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-266) Here, the term "attack against India" means attack against the "Union of India" or "Indian forces anywhere".[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-267)

Missile defence programme
-------------------------

India's missile defence network has two principal components – the Air Defence Ground Environment System (ADGES) and the Base Air Defence Zones (BADZ). The ADGES network provides for wide area radar coverage and permits the detection and interception of most aerial incursions into Indian airspace. The BADZ system is far more concentrated with [radars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radars "Radars"), [interceptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interceptor_aircraft "Interceptor aircraft"), [surface-to-air missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile") (SAMs) and [anti-aircraft artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-aircraft_artillery "Anti-aircraft artillery") (AAA) units working together to provide an intense and highly effective defensive barrier to attacks on vital targets.[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-BR-268)

### Ballistic missile defence

[![Image 111](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Bharat_BMD_Phase-II_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Bharat_BMD_Phase-II_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bharat_BMD_Phase-II_/(cropped/).jpg)

Second phase of Anti-ballistic Missile defence test with AD-1 missile

The Ballistic Missile Defence Program is an initiative to develop and deploy a multi-layered [ballistic missile defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_missile_defence "Ballistic missile defence") system to protect India from [ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_missile "Ballistic missile") attacks.[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IHT-269)[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-270)

Introduced in light of the ballistic missile threat from Pakistan,[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-271) it is a double-tiered system consisting of two [interceptor missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-ballistic_missile "Anti-ballistic missile"), namely the [Prithvi Air Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prithvi_Air_Defence "Prithvi Air Defence") (PAD) missile for high-altitude interception, and the [Advanced Air Defence (AAD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Air_Defence_/(AAD/) "Advanced Air Defence (AAD)") Missile for lower altitude interception. The two-tiered shield should be able to intercept any incoming missile launched 5,000 kilometres (3,100 mi) away.[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-272)

PAD was tested in November 2006, followed by AAD in December 2007. With the test of the PAD missile, India became the fourth country to have successfully developed an anti-ballistic missile system, after the United States, Russia and [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-273) On 6 March 2009, India again successfully tested its missile defence shield, during which an incoming "enemy" missile was intercepted at an altitude of 75 kilometres (47 mi).[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-274)

On 6 May 2012, it was announced that Phase-I is complete and can be deployed on short notice to protect Indian cities.[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-275)[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-thehindu.com-276) [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi"), the national capital, and [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"), have been selected for the ballistic missile defence shield.[\[274\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-277) After successful implementation in Delhi and Mumbai, the system will be used to cover other major cities in the country.[\[275\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-278) This shield can destroy incoming ballistic missiles launched from as far as 2,500 kilometres (1,600 mi) away. When the Phase II is completed and the PDV is developed, the two anti-ballistic missiles can intercept targets up to 5,000 kilometres (3,100 mi) both at exo and endo-atmospheric (inside the atmosphere) regions. The missiles will work in tandem to ensure a hit probability of 99.8 per cent.[\[276\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IBNLiveA-279)[\[277\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-280) This system can handle multiple targets simultaneously with multiple interceptors.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

India is reported to have procured a squadron of [S-300V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-300VM "S-300VM") systems which are in use as an anti-tactical ballistic missile screen.[\[278\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-BR-2-281)[\[279\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-DNews-282)

### Cruise missile defence

Defending against an attack by a cruise missile on the other hand is similar to tackling low-flying manned aircraft and hence most methods of aircraft defence can be used for a cruise missile defence system. To ward off the threats of nuclear-tipped cruise missile attack India has a new missile defence programme which will be focused solely on intercepting cruise missiles. The technological breakthrough has been created with an AAD missile.[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IBNLiveB-283) DRDO Chief, Dr. [V K Saraswat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_K_Saraswat "V K Saraswat") stated in an interview: "Our studies have indicated that this AAD will be able to handle a cruise missile intercept."[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IBNLiveB-283)

Furthermore, India is acquiring airborne radars like [AWACS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airborne_early_warning_and_control "Airborne early warning and control") to ensure detection of cruise missiles in order to stay on top of the threat.[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IBNLiveB-283)

[Barak-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barak-8 "Barak-8") is a long-range anti-air and anti-missile naval defence system being developed jointly by [Israel Aerospace Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Aerospace_Industries "Israel Aerospace Industries") (IAI) and the [Defence Research and Development Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Research_and_Development_Organisation "Defence Research and Development Organisation") (DRDO) of India.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-NT-284) The Indian Army is considering the induction of a variant of the Barak 8 missile to meet its requirement for a medium-range [surface-to-air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air "Surface-to-air") air defence missile. The naval version of this missile has the capability to intercept incoming enemy cruise missiles and combat jets targeting its warships at sea.[\[282\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IANS-285) It would also be inducted into the Indian Air Force, followed by the Army.[\[283\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-286) Recently developed, India's [Akash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akash_/(missile/) "Akash (missile)") missile defence system also has the capability to "neutralise aerial targets like fighter jets, cruise missiles and air-to-surface missiles".[\[284\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-287)[\[285\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-288) Both the Barak-8 and the Akash missile defence systems can engage multiple targets simultaneously during saturation attacks.[\[286\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IAI_PDF_%E2%80%93_Barak_8-289)

On 17 November 2010, in an interview Rafael's vice-president Mr. Lova Drori confirmed that the [David's Sling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David%27s_Sling "David's Sling") system has been offered to the Indian Armed Forces.[\[287\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-IDefence-290) This system is further designed to distinguish between decoys and the actual warhead of a missile.[\[288\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-291)

Defence intelligence
--------------------

The [Defence Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Intelligence_Agency_/(India/) "Defence Intelligence Agency (India)") (DIA) is an [organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_agency "Intelligence agency") responsible for providing and co-ordinating [intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_/(information_gathering/) "Intelligence (information gathering)") for the Indian armed forces.[\[290\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-MOD-293) It was created in March 2002 and is administered within the [Union Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_/(India/) "Ministry of Defence (India)").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] It is headed by a Director General who is also the principal adviser to the Minister of Defence and the Chief of Defence Staff.

Traditionally, the bulk of intelligence work in India has been carried out by the [Research and Analysis Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_Analysis_Wing "Research and Analysis Wing") (R&AW) and the [Intelligence Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_Bureau_/(India/) "Intelligence Bureau (India)") (IB). The various services intelligence directorates namely the Directorate of Military Intelligence (DMI), the Directorate of Air Intelligence (DAI), Directorate of Naval Intelligence (DNI) and some other agencies are also involved but their activity is smaller by comparison. The R&AW and IB agencies are composed largely of civilians. Military personnel are often deputed to these agencies, but the letter of the law and concerns of deniability limit the use of serving military officers in some types of activity (especially collection and action). The creation of an intelligence agency co-ordinating the intelligence arms of the three military services had long been called for by senior Indian military officers.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] It was formally recommended by the [Cabinet Group of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_the_Republic_of_India "Council of Ministers of the Republic of India"), headed by the then [Deputy Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Prime_Minister_of_India "Deputy Prime Minister of India") [Lal Krishna Advani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lal_Krishna_Advani "Lal Krishna Advani"). The Group of Ministers investigated intelligence lapses that occurred during the [Kargil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kargil_War "Kargil War") and recommended a comprehensive reform of [Indian intelligence agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Indian_Intelligence_agencies "List of Indian Intelligence agencies").[\[291\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-A-294) The Defence Intelligence Agency was created and became operational in March 2002.[\[291\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-A-294) As part of expanding bilateral co-operation on gathering intelligence and fighting terrorism, the [United States military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military "United States military") also provided advice to Indian military officers on the creation of the DIA.[\[291\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-A-294)

DIA has control of MoD's prized technical intelligence assets – the Directorate of Signals Intelligence and the Defence Image Processing and Analysis Centre (DIPAC). While the Signals Directorate is responsible for acquiring and decrypting enemy communications, the DIPAC controls India's satellite-based image acquisition capabilities. The DIA also controls the Defence Information Warfare Agency (DIWA) which handles all elements of the information warfare repertoire, including psychological operations, cyber-war, electronic intercepts and the monitoring of sound waves.

Research and development
------------------------

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is an agency of the Republic of India, responsible for the development of technology for use by the military, headquartered in New Delhi, India. It was formed in 1958 by the merger of the Technical Development Establishment and the Directorate of Technical Development and Production with the Defence Science Organisation. DRDO has a network of 52 laboratories which are engaged in developing defence technologies covering various fields, like aeronautics, armaments, electronic and computer sciences, human resource development, life sciences, materials, missiles, combat vehicles development and naval research and development. The organisation includes more than 5,000 scientists and about 25,000 other scientific, technical and supporting personnel. Annual operating budget of the DRDO is pegged at $1.6 billion (2011–12).[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-295)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\]

### Electronic-warfare, Cyber-warfare, military hardware

The DRDO's avionics programme has been a success story with its mission computers, [radar warning receivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_warning_receivers "Radar warning receivers"), high accuracy direction finding pods, [synthetic aperture radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_aperture_radar "Synthetic aperture radar"), [Active Phased Array Radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_Phased_Array_Radar "Active Phased Array Radar"), airborne jammers and flight instrumentation in use across a wide variety of Indian Air Force aircraft and satellites. DRDO labs have developed many [electronic warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare "Electronic warfare") systems for IAF and the Indian Army and high-performance [Sonar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonar "Sonar") systems for the navy.

DRDO also developed other critical military hardware, such as the [Arjun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_MBT "Arjun MBT") Main Battle Tank, and is engaged in the development of a future [Infantry Combat Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry_Combat_Vehicle "Infantry Combat Vehicle"). The DRDO is also a member of the trials teams for the T-72 upgrade and its fire control systems. [INSAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS "INSAS"), India's de facto standard small arms family including [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle"), [light machine guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_machine_guns "Light machine guns") and [carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbine "Carbine"), is developed at the [Armament Research and Development Establishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armament_Research_and_Development_Establishment "Armament Research and Development Establishment"), a DRDO laboratory. ARDE also worked on the development of [Pinaka Multi Barrel Rocket Launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinaka_Multi_Barrel_Rocket_Launcher "Pinaka Multi Barrel Rocket Launcher"), which has a maximum range of 39 kilometres (24 mi) – 40 kilometres (25 mi) and can fire a salvo of 12 high-explosive rockets in 44 seconds, neutralising a target area of 3.9 square km. This project was one of the first major Indian defence projects involving the Private sector.

India has created the [Defence Cyber Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Cyber_Agency "Defence Cyber Agency"), which has the responsibility of conducting [Cyberwarfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberwarfare "Cyberwarfare").[\[293\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-296)

[![Image 112](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Nag_with_NAMICA_Defexpo-2008.JPG/250px-Nag_with_NAMICA_Defexpo-2008.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nag_with_NAMICA_Defexpo-2008.JPG)

DRDO-built 3rd-generation [ATGM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATGM "ATGM") [Nag missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nag_missile "Nag missile").

DRDO executed the [Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Guided_Missile_Development_Programme "Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme") (IGMDP) to establish the ability to develop and design a missile locally, and manufacture a range of missile systems for the three defence services. The programme has seen significant success in its two most important constituents – the [Agni missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agni_/(missile/) "Agni (missile)") and the [Prithvi missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prithvi_/(missile/) "Prithvi (missile)"), while two other programmes, the [Akash SAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akash_SAM "Akash SAM") and the anti-tank [Nag Missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nag_Missile "Nag Missile") have seen significant orders. Another significant project of DRDO has been the [Astra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astra_/(missile/) "Astra (missile)") [beyond-visual-range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond-visual-range_missile "Beyond-visual-range missile") air-to-air missile (BVR), for equipping IAF's [air-superiority fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_superiority_fighter "Air superiority fighter"). The crown jewel of DRDO has been the [BrahMos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BrahMos "BrahMos") programme (as a joint venture with Russian NPO), which aims at creating a range of [supersonic cruise missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_missile "Cruise missile") derived from the [Yakhont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakhont "Yakhont") system. The DRDO has been responsible for the navigational systems on the BrahMos, aspects of its propulsion, airframe and seeker, fire control systems, mobile command posts and the Transporter Erector Launcher.

The US Department of Defence ([Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Defense_/(USA/) "Department of Defense (USA)")) has written to India's Ministry of Defence (MoD), proposing the two countries collaborate in jointly developing a next-generation version of the [Javelin anti-tank missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin_anti-tank_missile "Javelin anti-tank missile").[\[294\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-297)

### Unmanned aerial vehicles

[![Image 113](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Rustom_flight_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Rustom_flight_2_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rustom_flight_2_/(cropped/).jpg)

[TAPAS-BH-201](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAPAS-BH-201 "TAPAS-BH-201") MALE UAV.

The DRDO has also developed many [unmanned aerial vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_aerial_vehicles "Unmanned aerial vehicles")\- such as the [Nishant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DRDO_Nishant "DRDO Nishant") tactical UAV and the [Lakshya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakshya_PTA "Lakshya PTA") Pilotless Target Aircraft (PTA). The Lakshya PTA has been ordered by all three services for their gunnery target training requirements. Efforts are ongoing to develop the PTA further, with an improved all-digital flight control system, and a better turbojet engine. The DRDO is also going ahead with its plans to develop a new class of UAV, referred to by the HALE (High Altitude Long Endurance) and MALE (Medium Altitude Long Endurance) designations. The MALE UAV has been tentatively named the [Rustom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DRDO_Rustom "DRDO Rustom"), and will feature canards and carry a range of payloads, including optronic, radar, laser designators and ESM. The UAV will have conventional landing and take off capability. The HALE UAV will have features such as SATCOM links, allowing it to be commanded beyond line of sight. Other tentative plans speak of converting the LCA into an [unmanned combat aerial vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_combat_aerial_vehicle "Unmanned combat aerial vehicle") (UCAV),[\[295\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-298) and weaponising UAVs such as [AURA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DRDO_AURA "DRDO AURA").[\[296\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-299)

### Anti-satellite weapon

In 2010, the defence ministry drafted a 15-year "Technology Perspective and Roadmap", which held development of [ASAT weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-satellite_weapon "Anti-satellite weapon") "for electronic or physical destruction of satellites in both LEO (2,000-km altitude above earth's surface) and the higher geosynchronous orbit" as a thrust area in its long-term integrated perspective plan under the management of DRDO.[\[297\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-300) On 10 February 2010, [Defence Research and Development Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Research_and_Development_Organisation "Defence Research and Development Organisation") Director-General, and Scientific Advisor to the Defence Minister, Dr VK Saraswat stated that India had "all the building blocks necessary" to integrate an anti-satellite weapon to neutralise hostile satellites in [low earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_Orbit "Low Earth Orbit") and [polar orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_orbit "Polar orbit"). India is known to have been developing an exo-atmospheric kill vehicle that can be integrated with the missile to engage satellites.[\[298\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-301)

On 27 March 2019, India conducted the [first test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Indian_anti-satellite_missile_test "2019 Indian anti-satellite missile test") of an ASAT weapon.[\[299\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-302)

### Future programmes

#### Directed-energy weapons

It is also known that DRDO is working on a slew of [directed energy weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_energy_weapons "Directed energy weapons") (DEWs) and has identified DEWs, along with space security, cyber-security, and hypersonic vehicles/missiles as focus areas in the next 15 years.[\[300\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-303)

#### Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle

The Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle (HSTDV) is an unmanned [scramjet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scramjet "Scramjet") demonstration aircraft for [hypersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic "Hypersonic") flight ([Mach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number "Mach number") 6.5). The HSTDV program is run by the DRDO.[\[301\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-THEHINDU-304)

### United Nations peacekeeping

[![Image 114](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Les_Soldats_de_la_Paix_du_bataillon_indien_lors_d%27une_patrouille_de_domination_de_terrain_%C3%A0_travers_la_for%C3%AAt_de_Pitakongo_%2815143910694%29.jpg/330px-Les_Soldats_de_la_Paix_du_bataillon_indien_lors_d%27une_patrouille_de_domination_de_terrain_%C3%A0_travers_la_for%C3%AAt_de_Pitakongo_%2815143910694%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Les_Soldats_de_la_Paix_du_bataillon_indien_lors_d%27une_patrouille_de_domination_de_terrain_%C3%A0_travers_la_for%C3%AAt_de_Pitakongo_/(15143910694/).jpg)

[![Image 115](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/The_Blue_Berets%2C_We_Care_%2815847021980%29.jpg/330px-The_Blue_Berets%2C_We_Care_%2815847021980%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Blue_Berets,_We_Care_/(15847021980/).jpg)

Indian Army doctors attend to a child in [Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo").

India has been the largest troop contributor to [UN missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_peacekeeping_missions "UN peacekeeping missions") since their inception.[\[302\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-Tuteja-305) So far India has taken part in 43 peacekeeping missions with a total contribution exceeding 160,000 troops and a significant number of police personnel having been deployed.[\[303\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-306) \[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] India has so far, provided one Military Advisor (Lt Gen R K Mehta), one Police Adviser (Ms Kiran Bedi), one Deputy Military Adviser (Lt Gen Abhijit Guha), 14 Force Commanders and numerous Police Commissioners in various UN Missions.\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] The Indian Army has also contributed lady officers as Military Observers and Staff Officers apart from them forming part of Medical Units being deployed in UN Missions. The first all women contingent in a peacekeeping mission, was a Formed Police Unit from India, deployed in 2007 to the UN Operation in Liberia(UNMIL).[\[304\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-307) India has suffered 127 soldier deaths while serving on peacekeeping missions.[\[305\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-308)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] India has also provided army contingents performing a peacekeeping operation in Sri Lanka between 1987 and 1990 as the [Indian Peace Keeping Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Peace_Keeping_Force "Indian Peace Keeping Force").In November 1988, India also helped to restore the government of [Maumoon Abdul Gayoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumoon_Abdul_Gayoom "Maumoon Abdul Gayoom") in the [Maldives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maldives "Maldives") under [Operation Cactus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Cactus "Operation Cactus").[\[306\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-309) As of June 2013, about 8000 Indian UN peacekeepers, both men and women, are deployed in nine missions, including the Congo, South Sudan, Liberia, UNDOF, Haiti, Lebanon, Abeyi, Cyprus and Cote de Ivoire.[\[302\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-Tuteja-305)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\]

### Anti-piracy mission

India sought to augment its naval force in the Gulf of Aden by deploying the larger [INS _Mysore_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INS_Mysore_/(D60/) "INS Mysore (D60)") to patrol the area. Somalia also added India to its list of states, including the US and France, who are permitted to enter its territorial waters, extending up to 12 [nautical miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_mile "Nautical mile") (22 km; 14 mi) from the coastline, in an effort to check piracy.[\[307\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-ins-hp-310) An Indian naval official confirmed receipt of a letter acceding to India's prerogative to check such piracy. "We had put up a request before the Somali government to play a greater role in suppressing piracy in the Gulf of Aden in view of the United Nations resolution. The TFG government gave its nod recently."[\[308\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-311) In November 2008, an Indian navy warship destroyed a suspected Somali pirate vessel after it came under attack in the Gulf of Aden. In a report on Somalia submitted to the Security Council, UN Secretary-General [Ban Ki-moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Ki-moon "Ban Ki-moon") said "I welcome the decision of the governments of India and the Russian Federation to cooperate with the Transitional Federal Government of Somalia to fight piracy and armed robbery against ships." India also expressed the desire to deploy up to four more [warships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warships "Warships") in the region.[\[309\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-312)[\[310\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-313) On 2010-09-06, a team of [Indian marine commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MARCOS "MARCOS") (MARCOS) boarded MV Jag Arnav and overpowered attacking pirates – seven heavily armed Somalis and one Yemeni national. In the seven-year time frame India deployed 52 warships to combat piracy, which resulted in the area up to 65 degrees east being cleared of pirates.[\[311\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-314)

### Relief operations

[![Image 116](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Indian_Air_Force_Cheetah_helicopters_rescue_op_2015_Chennai_Flood.jpg/250px-Indian_Air_Force_Cheetah_helicopters_rescue_op_2015_Chennai_Flood.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indian_Air_Force_Cheetah_helicopters_rescue_op_2015_Chennai_Flood.jpg)

An Indian Air Force helicopter rescues stranded people during [2015 Chennai Floods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_South_Indian_floods#Chennai "2015 South Indian floods").

The Indian Air Force provides regular relief operation for food and medical facilities around the world using its [cargo aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargo_aircraft "Cargo aircraft") most notably the [Ilyushin Il-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-76 "Ilyushin Il-76"). The most recent relief operation of the IAF was in [Kyrgyzstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrgyzstan "Kyrgyzstan").[\[312\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-315)[\[313\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-316)\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] During the [2010 Ladakh floods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Ladakh_floods "2010 Ladakh floods"), two Ilyushin Il-76 and four Antonov-32 aircraft of the IAF carried 30 tonnes of load, which include 125 rescue and relief personnel, medicines, generators, tents, portable X-ray machines and emergency rescue kits. A MI-17 helicopter and Cheetah helicopter were used to increase the effectiveness of the rescue operations.[\[314\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-317) During the 2013 [Uttrakhand Floods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_North_India_floods "2013 North India floods"), the Indian armed forces took part in rescue operations. By 21 June 2013, the Army had deployed 10,000 soldiers and 11 helicopters, the navy had sent 45 naval divers, and the Air force had deployed 43 aircraft including 36 helicopters. From 17 to 30 June 2013, the IAF airlifted a total of 18,424 people – flying a total of 2,137 sorties and dropping/landing a total of 3,36,930 kg of relief material and equipment. The IAF participated in the rescue operation codenamed [Operation Raahat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Raahat "Operation Raahat") and evacuated more than 4640 Indian citizens (along with 960 foreign nationals from 41 countries) from [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen") during the [2015 military intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_military_intervention_in_Yemen "2015 military intervention in Yemen") by [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") and its allies in that country during the [Yemeni Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_Crisis_/(2011%E2%80%93present/) "Yemeni Crisis (2011–present)").[\[315\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-Kumar_2015-318)[\[316\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-onein2015-319)[\[317\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-The_Times2015-320)[\[318\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-Zee_Newsx2015-321)[\[319\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-http://www.hindustantimes.com/_2015-322)[\[320\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-The_Times_of_India15-323)

### IAF efforts in eclipse study

The Indian Air Force successfully undertook sorties to help Indian scientists study the total solar eclipse that took place on 23 July 2010. Two separate missions from Agra and Gwalior were flown along the path of the Moon's shadow, a mission that was deemed hugely successful by scientists associated with the experiment. While one [AN-32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonov_An-32 "Antonov An-32") transport aircraft carrying scientific equipment, cameras and scientists took off from Agra and landed back after a three-hour flight, a [Mirage-2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_2000 "Dassault Mirage 2000") trainer from Gwalior took images of the celestial spectacle from 40,000 feet (12,000 m). With weather being clear at such altitudes and coordinates planned by the IAF pilots, both the AN-32 and Mirage-2000 pilots were able to accomplish the mission successfully.[\[321\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-324)

### Indian Navy exploration

[![Image 117](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Indian_Navy_at_the_North_Pole.jpg/250px-Indian_Navy_at_the_North_Pole.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indian_Navy_at_the_North_Pole.jpg)

The Indian Navy expedition to [North Pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole "North Pole"), 2008.

The Indian Navy regularly conducts adventure expeditions. The sailing ship and training vessel INS Tarangini began circumnavigating the world on 23 January 2003, intending to foster good relations with other nations; she returned to India in May of the following year after visiting 36 ports in 18 nations. Lt. Cdr. M.S. Kohli led the Indian Navy's first successful expedition to Mount Everest in 1965. Another Navy team also successfully scaled Everest from the north face, the more technically challenging route.[\[322\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-325) An Indian Navy team comprising 11 members successfully completed an expedition to the [North Pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole "North Pole") in 2006.[\[323\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-326) The Indian Naval ensign first flew in Antarctica in 1981. The Indian Navy succeeded in Mission Dakshin Dhruv by traversing to the [South Pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pole "South Pole") on skis in 2006. With this historic expedition, they set the record for being the world's first military team to have successfully completed a ski traverse to the geographic south pole.[\[324\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-327)

Misconceptions in nomenclature
------------------------------

There are a number of uniformed forces in India apart from the Indian Armed Forces. All such forces are established under the acts of Parliament. They are: the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Reserve_Police_Force "Central Reserve Police Force"), the [Border Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force"), the [Indo-Tibetan Border Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Tibetan_Border_Police "Indo-Tibetan Border Police"), the [Central Industrial Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force"), the [Sashastra Seema Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sashastra_Seema_Bal "Sashastra Seema Bal"), the [Assam Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam_Rifles "Assam Rifles"), the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") under the [Ministry of Home Affairs (India)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Home_Affairs_/(India/) "Ministry of Home Affairs (India)"), the [Special Protection Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Protection_Group "Special Protection Group") under the [Cabinet Secretariat of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_Secretariat_of_India "Cabinet Secretariat of India"), the [Railway Protection Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Protection_Force "Railway Protection Force") under [Ministry of Railways (India)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Railways_/(India/) "Ministry of Railways (India)"), and the [Indian Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Coast_Guard "Indian Coast Guard") (ICG) under the [Ministry of Defence (India)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_/(India/) "Ministry of Defence (India)"). These forces are referred to as "Armed Force of the Union" in their respective acts, which means a force with armed capability and not necessarily "Armed Forces", the term as per international standards and conventionally referred to as "Army", "Navy" and "Air Force". The Supreme Court in its judgements reported in _AIR 1996 SC 1705_ held that the military service is only confined to three principal wings of the armed forces i.e. Army, Navy and Air Force. Further the Supreme Court of India in a case reported in _AIR 2000 SC 3948_ clarified that unless it is a service in the three principal wing of the Armed Forces, a force included in the expression "Armed forces of the Union" does not constitute part of the military service/military.[\[325\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-328) To differentiate from Armed Forces, Some of other forces were commonly referred to as Central Paramilitary Forces which caused confusion and give the impression of them being part of the military forces.

To remove such confusion, in 2011 the Ministry of Home Affairs adopted the uniform nomenclature of [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") for only five of its Primary Police organisations.[\[326\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-329)[\[327\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-330) These were formerly called as Paramilitary Forces. [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") are still incorrectly referred to as "Paramilitary Forces" in the media and in some correspondences. These forces are headed by officers from the [Indian Police Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service") and are under the [Ministry of Home Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Home_Affairs_/(India/) "Ministry of Home Affairs (India)").

Other uniform services are referred to by their names only such as: the Railway Protection Force, the NSG, the SPG, the ICG, the Assam Rifles etc., but not under any collective nomenclature. However, conventionally some forces are referred to as the [Paramilitary Forces of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary_Forces_of_India "Paramilitary Forces of India"), for example the [Assam Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam_Rifles "Assam Rifles"), the [SFF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Frontier_Force "Special Frontier Force") and the ICG.

The Indian Coast Guard is often confused incorrectly as being a part of the military forces due to the organisation being under the Ministry of Defence. The Supreme Court in its judgement has held that unless it is a service in the three principal wings of the Armed Forces, a force included in the expression "Armed forces of the Union" does not constitute part of military service/military. The Indian Coast Guard works closely with civilian agencies such as Customs, the Department of Fisheries, the Coastal Police etc. with its primary role being that of a non-military, maritime law enforcement agency.[\[328\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-331)[\[329\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-332) It is independent of the command and control of the Indian Navy. ICG was initially planned to be kept under the Ministry of Home Affairs but has been kept under the Ministry of Defence for better synergy since it is patterned like the navy.[\[330\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces#cite_note-333) The ICG does not take part in any protocol of military forces such as the President's Body Guard, ADCs, the Tri-Services Guard of Honour etc. Their recruitment is also not under the Combined Defence Services Exam/National Defence Academy Exam which is one of the prime modes of commissioning officers to the Armed Forces. Indian Coast Guard Officers continue to get their training with Indian Navy Officers since the ICG does not have its own training academy. Already a new [Indian Coast Guard Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Coast_Guard_Academy "Indian Coast Guard Academy") for training of their officers is under construction.\[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_\] Often ICG loses its credit for being incorrectly recognised as part of Indian military Forces and not as a unique independent force.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

A Vision for the Future
=======================

###### ![Image 3](https://forceindia.net/media/summer/Sanjiv-Krishan-Sood.jpg)**S.K. Sood (retd)**

The five Central Armed Police Forces, namely Border Security Force (BSF), Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) have well defined mandated tasks, each of which is extremely important in the security matrix of the country.

The BSF, ITBP & SSB are mandated to secure vast land borders of India with Pakistan, China, and Bangladesh during peace, besides, assisting the defence forces in their war efforts. The CRPF is a designated Internal Security force while the CISF was raised for security of Vital Areas (VAs) and Vital Points (VPs) including industrial installations. Its task has now been expanded to include private industrial installations also. Besides the mandated tasks, each of the above forces are also required to assist Civil authorities in maintaining Law and order whenever called upon to do so.

All these forces were raised over fifty years ago except SSB which was converted into a uniformed border guarding force in 2001. Over the period of time, these forces have evolved systems and procedures including adopting modern technology for carrying out operations. Modernisation however is an unending process, the scope of which must encompass other aspects of their functioning in order to improve overall efficiency.

**Border Guarding Forces**

The security of borders of India is particularly important in view of repeated attempts by militants and trans-border criminals to exploit border porosity to fuel trouble. Border guarding has evolved from mere border policing by state Armed Police forces up till mid-sixties to guarding by specialised forces. Punjab militancy compelled India to install fences along India-Pakistan Border in Punjab. Their success in Punjab resulted in fencing being erected all along the India-Pak border in nineties and subsequently along India-Bangladesh border.

The fence proved useful till the trans-border criminals learnt to negotiate it and thus it was decided to strengthen its obstacle value and reduce stress on troops by installing flood light and early warning systems. However, border guarding practices remained manpower intensive, due to the necessity of keeping the fence obstacle under observation and fire. The introduction of technology in shape of ‘Night Vision Devices’ and ‘Thermal Imagers’ failed to reduce the burden on men because these are dumb devices and require men to use them. Reactions to the threats observed through these devices is also restricted due to lack of corresponding physical mobility.

The spate of terrorist attacks, especially since 2016 in Pathankot, Nagrota and Uri and other places. has once again flagged the importance of modernisation. Consequently, the Government of India has been pushing for technological solutions on both Eastern and Western borders through Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System (CIBMS) project which aims at integrating technology with existing systems to minimise human error. The system is under trial for last five years initially in the western sector where it was in shape of a turnkey project by a foreign company. However, finding the project co
